distractors.C: Discarding the baseline throws away the shared analysis that makes the comparison fair; both branches should start from the same understanding.
distractors.D: Switching approaches midway in a single resumed session mixes their contexts rather than isolating them into parallel branches.

scenario: During a resumed investigation, you tell the agent: 'Only `auth/token.py` and `auth/refresh.py` changed since we last worked; everything else is unchanged.'
stem: What is the primary benefit of scoping the update to those two files?

options.text: It forces the agent to re-explore the whole repository to be safe against hidden side effects
It enables targeted re-analysis of the changed files instead of full re-exploration
It permanently deletes the agent's prior context for all other files to avoid stale reasoning
It converts the session into a forked branch automatically for the changed files

rationale.correct: Naming the specific changed files lets the agent do targeted re-analysis of just those files while trusting its still-valid prior understanding of everything else, avoiding costly full re-exploration.

distractors.A: The point of scoping is to avoid whole-repository re-exploration, not to trigger it.
distractors.C: Informing the agent of changes updates its understanding of those files; it does not wipe context for unchanged files.
distractors.D: Describing file changes has nothing to do with forking; forking is a separate `fork_session` operation.

scenario: A month-old session investigated a payments bug. Since then the payments module was rewritten, but the root-cause conclusion and the reproduction steps you documented remain accurate.
stem: What is the most reliable way to continue this work now?

options.text: Resume the old session unchanged so the agent keeps all its original tool results and context
Fork the old session so both the stale and current code paths are explored together
Start a fresh session and inject a structured summary of the valid conclusions and repro steps
Resume the old session and instruct the agent to ignore its own stale tool results from before

rationale.correct: Because the module was rewritten, the old session's tool results are stale even though your conclusions hold. Starting fresh and injecting a structured summary of the valid findings gives the agent accurate, current context to reason from.

distractors.A: Resuming unchanged keeps stale tool results that describe code that no longer exists, undermining the agent's reasoning.
distractors.B: Forking would carry the stale baseline into both branches; forking is for divergent exploration from a valid baseline, not for salvaging outdated context.
distractors.D: Telling a resumed agent to ignore its own tool results is unreliable; a fresh session with a curated summary removes the stale results entirely rather than hoping they are disregarded.

scenario: Your internal knowledge-base agent exposes two tools, `search_docs` ("Search documents") and `search_tickets` ("Search tickets"), which accept similar free-text and identifier inputs. Logs show the agent frequently calls `search_docs` for support-ticket questions like "what's the status of TICK-4821?"
stem: What is the most effective first step to improve tool-selection reliability?

options.text: Add 6-8 few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating ticket queries routing to `search_tickets`.
Expand each tool's description: purpose, input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it versus the other.
Add a routing layer that parses each user message for keywords and identifier patterns and pre-selects the tool before the turn.
Consolidate both tools into a single `search_kb` tool that accepts any query and internally decides which backend to hit.

rationale.correct: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism an LLM uses for tool selection. When descriptions are minimal, the model lacks the context to differentiate between similar tools. Expanding them with purpose, input formats, example queries, edge cases, and explicit boundaries directly addresses the root cause and is the low-effort, high-leverage first step.

distractors.A: Few-shot examples add token overhead on every turn and paper over the real problem; the minimal descriptions remain the underlying cause of the misrouting.
distractors.C: A keyword-parsing routing layer is over-engineered for a 'first step' and bypasses the model's own natural-language understanding rather than fixing the descriptions that drive selection.
distractors.D: Consolidating tools is a valid architectural option but is heavier than a first step warrants when the immediate cause is inadequate descriptions, and it hides the backend distinction the model could otherwise reason about.

scenario: An agent has `analyze_content` ("Analyzes content and returns findings") and `analyze_document` ("Analyzes a document and returns findings"). The two descriptions are nearly identical, and in practice `analyze_content` only ever processes scraped web-search result pages while `analyze_document` handles uploaded PDFs. The agent routes inputs to the two tools unpredictably.
stem: Which remediation most directly fixes the misrouting?

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt pairing sample inputs with the tool that should handle them.
Give both tools identical input schemas so it no longer matters which one the model picks for a request.
Rename and rescope the tools to distinct purposes, e.g., `analyze_content` becomes `extract_web_results`.
Merge the two into one `analyze` tool that accepts any input type and detects the format itself.

rationale.correct: Near-identical descriptions are the classic cause of misrouting between overlapping tools. Renaming and rescoping so each tool signals a distinct purpose (for example `extract_web_results` with a web-specific description versus a document-specific one) removes the ambiguity the model was choosing between and is the fix the exam guide names for exactly this `analyze_content` vs `analyze_document` case.

distractors.A: Few-shot examples treat the symptom on each turn while leaving two indistinguishable descriptions in place; the model still has no principled basis to choose.
distractors.B: Making the schemas identical increases interchangeability and worsens the ambiguity; it does nothing to give each tool a differentiated purpose.
distractors.D: Merging into one generic `analyze` tool discards the meaningful web-versus-document distinction the system actually needs, trading a routing problem for an under-specified single tool.

scenario: Your tool descriptions are detailed and well-differentiated, yet the agent still over-calls `web_search` even for questions answerable from an attached document. Reviewing the system prompt, you find the line: "For any user request, always research the topic thoroughly before answering."
stem: What is the most likely cause of the unwanted `web_search` calls?

options.text: The system prompt's keyword-sensitive wording ("research the topic") biases the model toward `web_search`.
The `web_search` description is too long, so the model defaults to it whenever it is uncertain which tool fits.
`tool_choice` is set to `"any"`, which forces the model to make a tool call on every single turn.
The agent has too few tools, so it reuses `web_search` for tasks other tools should handle.

rationale.correct: System prompt wording can override even well-crafted tool descriptions. Keyword-sensitive phrasing like "research the topic" creates a strong, unintended association with the search tool, so the model reaches for `web_search` regardless of the descriptions. Reviewing and rewording the system prompt to remove the keyword bias is the fix.

distractors.B: Description length is not what is steering selection here; a thorough description is desirable, and the observed bias tracks the system prompt wording, not description size.
distractors.C: `tool_choice: "any"` would force some tool to be called but would not preferentially select `web_search` over other available tools; it does not explain the specific bias.
distractors.D: The scenario states other suitable tools exist and are well-described; tool scarcity is not the issue, the prompt's keyword association is.

scenario: A single generic `analyze_document` tool is asked, depending on context, to pull out structured data points, to produce a prose summary, or to check whether a specific claim is supported by the source. Its output shape varies run to run, and downstream steps that expect one shape often break.
stem: Which redesign best follows tool-interface best practices for this situation?

options.text: Keep the single tool but add several few-shot examples showing each kind of analysis.
Rename the tool to `process_document` and expand its description to cover all three behaviors.
Keep the single tool and add a required `mode` enum parameter (`data` / `summary` / `verify`) that the caller sets.
Split it into purpose-specific tools (`extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, `verify_claim_against_source`).

rationale.correct: A generic tool that does three different jobs produces ambiguous selection and inconsistent outputs. The recommended fix is to split it into purpose-specific tools such as `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, and `verify_claim_against_source`, each with a clear purpose and a defined input/output contract, so the model selects reliably and downstream steps get a predictable shape.

distractors.A: Few-shot examples do not fix the fact that one tool still owns three distinct contracts with one variable output shape; the ambiguity and downstream breakage remain.
distractors.B: Renaming to `process_document` and broadening the description makes the tool even more generic, deepening the very overlap and output-shape problem it should resolve.
distractors.C: A `mode` enum keeps three contracts inside one tool and one shared output shape; it partially disambiguates intent but still lets the model pick the wrong mode and does not give each behavior its own defined contract the way separate tools do.

stem: You are writing the description for a new tool that will sit alongside several similar tools. Which content makes the description most effective for reliable tool selection?

options.text: A single terse line ("Gets data") to minimize token usage and keep the tool definition compact.
Its purpose, accepted input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it versus similar tools.
A walkthrough of the tool's internal implementation and which backend service and database tables it queries.
An exhaustive list of every error code the tool can return, with no statement of its purpose.

rationale.correct: Because descriptions are the primary selection signal, an effective one differentiates the tool by stating its purpose, expected input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries clarifying when to use it versus similar tools. That is precisely the information the model needs to route correctly among alternatives.

distractors.A: A terse one-liner is the minimal-description anti-pattern; saving a few tokens comes at the cost of unreliable selection among similar tools.
distractors.C: Internal implementation and backend details do not help the model decide when to call the tool; the description should describe behavior and applicability, not plumbing.
distractors.D: An error-code catalog with no purpose statement gives the model nothing to select on; error handling is a separate concern from the selection cues a description must provide.

scenario: A tool named `analyze_content` in fact only parses search-engine result pages and returns the extracted hits, but its generic name and description ("Analyzes content") lead the agent to route uploaded PDFs and raw user text to it, producing failures.
stem: Which change best resolves the mismatch between the tool's name and its actual, narrow function?

options.text: Keep the name `analyze_content` but append a sentence to the description noting it is 'mainly for web results.'
Rename it to the broader `analyze_data` so its name clearly signals it accepts any content type.
Rename it to `extract_web_results` with a description stating it parses search-engine result pages.
Delete the tool and let the agent handle web-result parsing without a dedicated tool.

rationale.correct: When a tool's name and description are more generic than its real function, they invite misrouting. Renaming to something specific like `extract_web_results` with a web-results-specific description aligns the interface with the actual behavior, so the model stops sending PDFs and raw text to it.

distractors.A: Bolting a hedging phrase onto a still-generic name leaves the misleading `analyze_content` label in place; the model will keep treating it as a general analyzer.
distractors.B: Renaming to `analyze_data` makes the tool sound even broader than its narrow web-parsing function, worsening the mismatch rather than fixing it.
distractors.D: Deleting a correctly functioning, useful tool throws away needed capability; the problem is the misleading interface, not the tool's existence.

stem: Which statement best captures the foundational principle behind designing tool interfaces for reliable selection?

options.text: Tool descriptions are the primary selection mechanism; minimal descriptions make selection unreliable among similar tools.
The model selects tools primarily by their order in the tools array, so the most important tool belongs at the top of the list.
The model selects tools primarily by parameter count, preferring tools with fewer required parameters.
Tool selection is driven entirely by the system prompt; the model ignores tool descriptions once the prompt is set.

rationale.correct: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to choose among tools. Minimal or vague descriptions deprive it of the context needed to differentiate similar tools, which is why investing in clear, differentiated descriptions is the highest-leverage interface-design practice.

distractors.B: Array order is not the selection driver; relying on positioning instead of descriptive content leads to unreliable choices.
distractors.C: Parameter count does not determine selection; the model reasons about a tool's described purpose and applicability, not how many arguments it takes.
distractors.D: The system prompt influences behavior and can even bias selection, but it does not replace tool descriptions; descriptions remain the primary selection signal the model reads.

scenario: A banking agent has `get_account_balance` and `get_transaction_history`, both accepting an account ID. Each description accurately says what it returns, but neither says when to prefer one over the other. The agent often calls `get_account_balance` for requests like "show me my recent activity," returning a single number instead of a transaction list.
stem: Which addition to the tool descriptions would most improve differentiation between the two tools?

options.text: Shorten both descriptions to one line each so the model is not distracted by extra detail.
Give both tools identically named parameters so their interfaces look consistent to the model.
Add an external routing classifier that inspects each request and forces the tool choice before the model runs.
Add when-to-use-versus-the-other boundary statements and example queries for each tool.

rationale.correct: The descriptions state outputs but omit boundaries, so the model cannot tell which tool a request maps to. Adding explicit when-to-use-versus-the-other boundary statements and example queries that map intents (e.g., "recent activity" to `get_transaction_history`, "current balance" to balance) gives the model the differentiating cues it needs, which is exactly the boundary and example guidance effective descriptions should carry.

distractors.A: Shortening the descriptions removes information; the problem is too little differentiating detail, not too much, so this makes selection less reliable.
distractors.B: Identical parameter names increase how interchangeable the tools appear and do nothing to convey when each should be used; the ambiguity is in intent, not parameter naming.
distractors.C: An external routing classifier bypasses the model's own selection instead of fixing the descriptions, and it is disproportionate when the descriptions simply lack boundary and example guidance.

scenario: You are implementing an MCP tool `query_inventory` that wraps a backend service. Sometimes the backend is briefly unavailable, sometimes the caller passes a malformed SKU, and sometimes the query simply matches no rows.
stem: According to the MCP tool-response pattern, how should the tool signal a backend failure back to the calling agent?

options.text: Raise a native exception inside the tool handler and let it bubble up out of the MCP server process, relying on the transport layer to surface it.
Always return content with no error indicator, embedding the words "error" or "success" in a free-text string the agent can read.
Return a tool result with `isError: true` and content describing the failure, so the agent can reason about recovery.
Return an empty content array with no flags, since the absence of results implicitly tells the agent something went wrong.

rationale.correct: MCP tools communicate failures back to the agent by returning a result with `isError: true` alongside content describing what happened. This keeps the failure inside the normal tool-result channel where the model can see it and decide how to recover, rather than crashing the server or hiding the failure in prose.

distractors.A: Letting a native exception escape the handler breaks the MCP contract: the failure is not delivered as a structured tool result the agent can reason over, and it can destabilize the server rather than informing the model.
distractors.B: Free-text "error"/"success" strings with no `isError` flag force the agent to guess from prose whether the call failed; the structured `isError` flag is precisely what removes that ambiguity.
distractors.D: An empty result with no flag is indistinguishable from a valid empty query result; conflating access failures with successful no-match responses prevents correct recovery decisions.

scenario: A payments MCP tool can fail in several ways: the downstream gateway times out, the caller supplies an amount in the wrong currency format, the transaction exceeds the customer's daily limit, or the API key lacks the required scope.
stem: Which classification correctly maps these four failures to error categories the agent can act on?

options.text: Gateway timeout = transient; wrong currency format = validation; over daily limit = business; missing key scope = permission.
Gateway timeout = validation; wrong currency format = transient; over daily limit = permission; missing key scope = business.
All four are transient errors, since any of them might succeed if the agent simply tries the call again later.
Gateway timeout = permission; wrong currency format = business; over daily limit = validation; missing key scope = transient.

rationale.correct: Each failure maps to a distinct category with different recovery implications: a gateway timeout is transient (worth retrying), a malformed currency is a validation error (the input must be corrected), exceeding the daily limit is a business/policy violation (retrying will not help), and an insufficient key scope is a permission error (needs elevated access). Correct categorization is what lets the agent choose the right recovery.

distractors.B: This scrambles the categories: a timeout is not a validation error, and a malformed input is not transient. Miscategorizing them would lead the agent to retry inputs that will never validate and to give up on failures that would succeed on retry.
distractors.C: Treating all failures as transient causes the agent to waste retries on validation, business, and permission failures that are deterministic and will fail identically every time.
distractors.D: This assignment is inverted across the board; for example, marking a timeout as permission and a missing scope as transient sends the agent into retry loops on non-retryable auth failures.

scenario: Every tool in a codebase returns the same failure payload: `{ isError: true, content: "Operation failed" }`. A reviewer flags this as an anti-pattern.
stem: What is the primary problem with returning a uniform, generic "Operation failed" message for every error?

options.text: It is slightly larger over the wire than a bare status code, marginally increasing latency on each failed tool call.
It gives the agent no signal about failure category or retryability, so it cannot choose an appropriate recovery.
It violates the MCP schema, because the `isError` flag may not be paired with a human-readable string.
It prevents the tool from ever setting `isError` to `true` on subsequent calls within the same session.

rationale.correct: A uniform "Operation failed" collapses transient, validation, business, and permission failures into one indistinguishable response. The agent loses the information it needs to decide whether to retry, correct input, or surface a customer-facing explanation, so recovery degrades to blind retries or premature failure.

distractors.A: The problem is informational, not about payload size or latency; a few extra bytes are irrelevant compared to losing all recovery signal.
distractors.C: Pairing `isError: true` with a human-readable string is valid and in fact encouraged; the issue is that the string is uninformative, not that it is present.
distractors.D: The `isError` flag can be set independently on each call; a generic message on one call does not disable the flag later. This is not the reason it is an anti-pattern.

scenario: An agent calls a tool that fails with a validation error (an invalid date range). Because the error payload carries no retry metadata, the agent retries the identical call five times before giving up.
stem: What single piece of structured metadata would most directly have prevented these wasted retries?

options.text: A timestamp on the error so the agent could rate-limit its retries to one per second.
A full stack trace so the agent could locate the exact line that threw and diagnose the cause.
A correlation ID so the retries could be grouped together in observability tooling.
An `isRetryable: false` flag marking the failure as deterministic and non-transient.

rationale.correct: The retries are wasted because the agent had no way to know the failure was non-retryable. An explicit `isRetryable: false` (or `retriable: false`) flag communicates that the error is deterministic; retrying the same input will fail the same way, so the agent should fix the input or halt rather than loop.

distractors.A: A timestamp only paces the retries; it does not tell the agent that retrying is pointless, so the wasted attempts still happen.
distractors.B: A stack trace aids human debugging but does not give the agent a machine-actionable retry decision; the agent would still retry a validation failure.
distractors.C: A correlation ID improves observability of the retries but does nothing to prevent them, since it carries no retryability signal.

scenario: You are designing the error contract for a fleet of MCP tools so that a coordinating agent can recover intelligently and, when needed, explain failures to an end user.
stem: Which error-response shape best equips the agent to both recover programmatically and communicate clearly?

options.text: `{ isError: true, errorCategory: "transient", isRetryable: true, message: "Inventory service timed out." }`
`{ isError: true, content: "Operation failed" }` — a flag plus a single generic string that fits every failure.
`{ error: true }` — a minimal boolean so the payload stays small and the agent can decide everything from context.
`{ isError: true, code: 500 }` — a numeric code the agent can look up, without any category or retry hint.

rationale.correct: The strongest contract combines a machine-readable `errorCategory`, an explicit `isRetryable` boolean, and a human-readable `message`. The category and retry flag drive programmatic recovery, while the message lets the agent explain the situation to a user without leaking internals or guessing.

distractors.B: The generic "Operation failed" string carries no category or retry signal, so it cannot support informed recovery or a meaningful explanation.
distractors.C: A bare boolean tells the agent only that something failed, forcing it to guess the category and retryability from context it does not have.
distractors.D: A raw numeric code with no category or retry hint pushes the agent to infer meaning from HTTP status conventions that may not map cleanly to transient/validation/business/permission distinctions.

scenario: A `submit_refund` MCP tool rejects a request because the order is outside the 30-day refund window — a firm company policy. The agent is customer-facing.
stem: How should the tool structure this business-rule failure so the agent behaves correctly?

options.text: Return `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "transient"` and `isRetryable: true`, letting the agent retry a few times in case the window recalculates.
Return a normal successful result with an empty body, since no refund was created and there is technically nothing to report.
Return `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "business"`, `retriable: false`, and a customer-friendly message explaining the 30-day window.
Return `isError: true` with only an internal policy identifier like `POLICY_REFUND_WINDOW_EXCEEDED` and no human-readable text, so the agent forwards the code verbatim.

rationale.correct: A policy violation is a business error that will not change on retry, so it should carry `retriable: false` and a `business` category. Pairing that with a customer-friendly explanation (e.g., "This order is past the 30-day refund window and is not eligible for a refund.") lets the agent communicate the outcome appropriately instead of retrying or exposing internals.

distractors.A: Labeling a firm policy rejection as transient and retryable sends the agent into pointless retries of a deterministic failure that will never succeed.
distractors.B: Marking the rejection as a successful empty result hides the failure; the agent may report that the refund succeeded or silently do nothing, misleading the customer.
distractors.D: An internal-only code with no human-readable text forces the agent to relay an opaque identifier to the customer, producing a confusing, non-customer-friendly explanation.

scenario: A research subagent issues several web searches for a coordinator. One search hits a transient timeout, two succeed, and one returns partial data before the connection drops.
stem: How should the subagent handle these failures before deciding what to send back to the coordinator?

options.text: Immediately propagate every individual failure to the coordinator without attempting any local handling, so the coordinator owns all recovery.
Retry the transient timeout locally, and propagate to the coordinator only what it cannot resolve, with partial results and what was attempted.
Discard the partial results and the timed-out search, returning only the two clean successes so the coordinator sees a tidy response.
Catch all failures locally and return an all-successful result to the coordinator regardless of what actually failed, to keep the pipeline moving.

rationale.correct: The subagent should resolve transient failures locally where it can (e.g., a bounded retry on the timeout) and escalate to the coordinator only failures it cannot resolve, packaging partial results and a note on what was attempted. This gives the coordinator the context to decide whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative, or proceed with partial data.

distractors.A: Propagating every raw failure without local handling floods the coordinator with noise it could have avoided and forfeits the subagent's ability to recover transient issues close to their source.
distractors.C: Silently dropping the partial results and the failed search hides information the coordinator needs; it may conclude the research was complete when it was not.
distractors.D: Reporting all-successful when work actually failed suppresses the error entirely, preventing any recovery and risking incomplete or inaccurate downstream synthesis.

scenario: A `search_customers` MCP tool runs a query that executes successfully but matches zero customers. Separately, on another call, the customer database is unreachable.
stem: How should the tool distinguish these two outcomes in its responses?

options.text: Return `isError: true` for both, since in both cases the agent received no usable customer records.
Return a successful, non-error result for both, distinguishing them only by whether the content string mentions the word "unreachable."
Return `isError: true` for the zero-match case (nothing was found) and a successful empty result when the database is unreachable (no exception was raised to the caller).
Return a successful empty list for the zero-match query, and `isError: true` with `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` for the unreachable database.

rationale.correct: A zero-match query is a valid, successful result and should be returned as a normal empty list, so the agent reports "no matching customers" with confidence. An unreachable database is an access failure and must be flagged with `isError: true` plus category and retry metadata, so the agent knows to retry or escalate rather than concluding no customers exist.

distractors.A: Flagging a valid empty result as an error causes the agent to treat a correct "no matches" answer as a failure, triggering needless retries or false error reports to the user.
distractors.B: Marking both as successful and distinguishing them only by scanning prose forces the agent to guess; the access failure would be mistaken for a genuine empty result.
distractors.C: This is inverted: the zero-match case is a success, not an error, and the unreachable database is a real access failure that must not be reported as a successful empty result.

scenario: A research agent in your multi-agent system has been given all 18 tools exposed by the platform so it can 'handle anything.' Its teammates each carry 4-5 role-specific tools. Testing shows the 18-tool agent increasingly picks the wrong tool, chains redundant calls, and stalls on decisions.
stem: What is the most likely root cause of the degraded tool selection, and the correct remedy?

options.text: The context window is too small for 18 schemas; upgrade to a larger-context model so every tool definition fits comfortably.
Too many tools increases decision complexity and degrades selection; restrict the agent to the 4-5 tools its role actually needs.
The tool descriptions are too short; expand every one of the 18 descriptions with more detail so the model can disambiguate them.
The agent lacks an explicit ordering hint; add a numbered priority list of all 18 tools to the system prompt so it checks them in order.

rationale.correct: Giving one agent far more tools than its role requires (18 versus a focused 4-5) increases decision complexity and measurably degrades selection reliability. Scoping the agent to only the tools relevant to its role restores reliable selection.

distractors.A: The problem is decision complexity across too many options, not schema size against the context window; a larger context does not make the model choose better among 18 overlapping tools.
distractors.C: Longer descriptions can help disambiguate genuinely needed tools, but they do not solve the core issue that the agent simply has too many tools for its role; the fix is fewer tools, not more prose.
distractors.D: Hard-coding a priority list fights the model's dynamic, context-driven selection and does not reduce the underlying decision space; the correct move is to remove tools the role does not need.

scenario: Your synthesis agent's job is to combine findings from other agents into a coherent report. Because it was given the web search tools 'just in case,' it now frequently launches its own searches mid-synthesis, producing inconsistent, off-scope results instead of synthesizing what it was handed.
stem: Which principle best explains this failure and points to the fix?

options.text: Agents given tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them; remove the web search tools from the synthesis agent so it stays within its role.
The synthesis agent needs a higher temperature to explore alternatives; lower the temperature and the misuse will stop.
The coordinator is delegating incorrectly; move all synthesis work into the coordinator so no separate agent holds search tools.
The web search tools are poorly documented; rewriting their descriptions will stop the synthesis agent from calling them inappropriately.

rationale.correct: Agents equipped with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them, exactly as the synthesis agent does when it runs its own searches instead of synthesizing. Restricting each agent's tool set to its role prevents this cross-specialization misuse.

distractors.B: Temperature governs sampling randomness, not whether an agent has and reaches for out-of-role tools; the misuse stems from the tool being available at all.
distractors.C: Collapsing synthesis into the coordinator abandons useful separation of concerns; the targeted fix is to scope the synthesis agent's tools, not to eliminate the role.
distractors.D: Better descriptions do not remove the temptation to use an out-of-specialization tool; the agent should not hold web search tools in the first place.

scenario: A document-analysis agent currently uses a generic `fetch_url` tool. Occasionally it fetches arbitrary or malformed URLs, pulling in irrelevant web pages instead of the approved document repository, which corrupts downstream analysis.
stem: What is the most effective way to constrain this agent's fetching behavior?

options.text: Keep `fetch_url` but add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to only fetch approved document URLs.
Remove all fetching capability and require a human to paste document contents into the prompt each time.
Replace the generic `fetch_url` with a constrained `load_document` tool that validates document URLs.
Set `tool_choice` to `"any"` so the model is forced to always call `fetch_url` on every turn.

rationale.correct: Replacing a broad, generic tool with a constrained alternative is the recommended pattern: a `load_document` tool that validates document URLs structurally prevents the agent from reaching arbitrary or malformed pages, rather than relying on the model to police itself.

distractors.A: A prompt rule is a soft guardrail the model can still violate; the generic tool's capability surface is unchanged, so malformed or off-repository fetches remain possible.
distractors.B: Eliminating automated fetching cripples the agent and forces manual work; the goal is a constrained tool, not the removal of the capability.
distractors.D: `tool_choice: "any"` only guarantees that some tool is called; it does not constrain which URLs `fetch_url` accepts and would actually force more indiscriminate fetching.

scenario: During testing, the synthesis agent frequently needs to verify simple claims (dates, names, statistics) while combining findings. Today it returns control to the coordinator, which invokes the web search agent and re-invokes synthesis, adding 2-3 round trips and 40% latency. Evaluation shows 85% of verifications are simple fact-checks and 15% require deeper investigation.
stem: What is the most effective way to reduce overhead while maintaining reliability?

options.text: Give the synthesis agent the full web search toolset so it can run every verification itself and skip the coordinator round-trips entirely.
Give the synthesis agent a scoped `verify_fact` tool for simple lookups, while complex verifications still route through the coordinator to the web search agent.
Have the synthesis agent batch all verification needs and return them to the coordinator at the end of its pass, so a single web-search sweep resolves them together.
Have the web search agent proactively cache extra context around each source, anticipating what synthesis might later need to verify.

rationale.correct: A scoped cross-role tool like `verify_fact` handles the 85% high-frequency simple case in-place while complex cases still route through the coordinator to the web search agent. This applies least privilege: the synthesis agent gets exactly the narrow capability it needs, not the whole search toolset.

distractors.A: Handing the synthesis agent the full search toolset over-provisions it and reintroduces cross-specialization misuse, violating separation of concerns.
distractors.C: Batching creates blocking dependencies because later synthesis steps may depend on facts verified earlier; deferring all verification to the end breaks that ordering.
distractors.D: Speculative caching cannot reliably predict which specific claims synthesis will need to verify, so it wastes work without dependably eliminating round-trips.

scenario: You are building a data-extraction step that must always emit a structured tool call so a downstream pipeline can parse the result. Occasionally the model instead replies with conversational text ('Sure, here is the data...') and the pipeline breaks because no tool was invoked.
stem: Which `tool_choice` setting guarantees the model calls a tool rather than returning free text, while still letting it choose which tool?

options.text: `tool_choice: "auto"`, since auto mode always prefers tools over text when tools are defined.
`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_data"}`, because only forced single-tool selection can prevent text.
No `tool_choice` setting; add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to never reply with text.
`tool_choice: "any"`, which requires some tool call but leaves the choice of tool to the model.

rationale.correct: `tool_choice: "any"` guarantees the model calls a tool rather than producing conversational text, while still letting it decide which tool best fits the input — exactly the requirement here. Model support: forced tool use (`"any"` or a named tool) works on most Claude models, but the newest ones (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) reject it with a 400. There, get the same guarantee with `"auto"` plus a prompt instruction naming the tool and `strict: true` on its schema, or with structured outputs (`output_config.format`).

distractors.A: `"auto"` lets the model decide whether to call a tool or reply with text, so it does not guarantee a tool call and would still allow the conversational replies that break the pipeline.
distractors.B: Forcing a single named tool does guarantee a tool call, but it removes the model's ability to choose among tools; the scenario only requires that some tool be called, so this is more restrictive than needed.
distractors.C: A prompt instruction is a soft guardrail the model can ignore; it does not structurally guarantee a tool call the way `"any"` does.

scenario: An enrichment agent must always run `extract_metadata` first so its output (document type, dates, author) is available before any enrichment tools fire. In practice the model sometimes jumps straight to enrichment tools and skips metadata extraction, producing incomplete records.
stem: What is the correct way to guarantee `extract_metadata` is the first tool called, then continue the workflow?

options.text: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first turn, then use `"auto"` for follow-ups.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` and hope the model happens to pick `extract_metadata` before the others.
Set `tool_choice: "auto"` and add 'always call extract_metadata first' to the system prompt.
Remove all enrichment tools until after metadata is extracted, then re-add them by editing the running request.

rationale.correct: Forced tool selection, `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`, guarantees that specific tool is called first. You then process subsequent steps in follow-up turns (for example switching to `"auto"`) so enrichment proceeds after metadata exists. Model support: forced tool use (`"any"` or a named tool) works on most Claude models, but the newest ones (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) reject it with a 400. There, get the same guarantee with `"auto"` plus a prompt instruction naming the tool and `strict: true` on its schema, or with structured outputs (`output_config.format`).

distractors.B: `"any"` guarantees only that some tool is called, not which one, so the model could still call an enrichment tool before `extract_metadata`.
distractors.C: `"auto"` plus a prompt instruction is a soft ordering hint the model can skip; it does not guarantee metadata extraction runs first.
distractors.D: Dynamically stripping and re-adding tools mid-request is not the intended mechanism; forced `tool_choice` on the first turn is the direct, supported way to guarantee ordering.

scenario: A general-purpose coding assistant should be free to answer some requests conversationally (explaining a concept) and use tools for others (reading or editing a file), deciding case by case based on the user's message.
stem: Which `tool_choice` mode fits this behavior?

options.text: `"any"`, so each response includes at least one tool call and the assistant stays action-oriented.
`{"type": "tool", "name": "read_file"}`, forcing a file read each turn so answers stay grounded in the code.
`"auto"`, letting the model decide each turn whether to call a tool or reply in text.
Disable tools entirely and have the model describe the edits it would make for the user to apply.

rationale.correct: `tool_choice: "auto"` lets the model decide, turn by turn, whether to call a tool or reply with text. That matches an assistant that should sometimes explain conversationally and sometimes act via tools.

distractors.A: `"any"` forces a tool call on every turn, so the assistant could never simply explain a concept in text — the wrong fit for mixed conversational/tool behavior.
distractors.B: Forcing `read_file` every turn makes the assistant read a file even when the user only asked a conceptual question.
distractors.D: Disabling tools removes the ability to read or edit files at all, defeating the assistant's purpose.

scenario: You are finalizing tool distribution for a hub-and-spoke system: a coordinator, a web search agent, a document-analysis agent, and a synthesis agent. A teammate proposes giving every agent the same broad tool set 'for flexibility,' plus setting `tool_choice: "any"` everywhere to 'keep them productive.'
stem: Which critique of this proposal is most accurate?

options.text: The proposal is sound: uniform broad tools maximize flexibility, and `"any"` prevents idle conversational turns across all agents.
Only the `tool_choice` part is wrong; giving all agents identical broad tool sets is a best practice for resilience.
Only the tool distribution is wrong; `tool_choice: "any"` is always the safest default for every agent.
Both parts are flawed: broad uniform tool sets degrade selection, and blanket `"any"` forces tool calls when text fits better.

rationale.correct: Both ideas are anti-patterns. Uniform broad tool sets raise decision complexity (degrading selection) and let agents misuse out-of-role tools; blanket `tool_choice: "any"` forces a tool call even when text or reasoning is appropriate. The right design scopes each agent's tools to its role and chooses the `tool_choice` mode (`"auto"`, `"any"`, or forced) that fits each agent's job.

distractors.A: Uniform broad tools are precisely what degrades selection reliability and enables cross-specialization misuse, so the proposal is not sound.
distractors.B: Identical broad tool sets are not a resilience best practice; over-provisioning tools harms selection just as much as the `tool_choice` mistake.
distractors.C: `"any"` is not a universally safe default; it forces a tool call even when an agent should respond conversationally, so the `tool_choice` half is also flawed.

scenario: Your team wants every engineer who clones the repository to automatically get access to the same internal GitHub and Sentry MCP servers, with no per-person setup steps.
stem: Where should you define these MCP servers so the configuration is shared with the whole team through version control?

options.text: In a project-level `.mcp.json` file committed to the repository root.
In each developer's user-level `~/.claude.json`, copied by hand during onboarding.
In a `CLAUDE.md` block that lists the server commands as documentation.
In environment variables exported from each developer's shell profile.

rationale.correct: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` at the repository root is designed for shared team tooling: because it is committed to version control, every teammate who clones the repo automatically inherits the same MCP server definitions without manual setup.

distractors.B: `~/.claude.json` is user-scoped and personal; it is not shared through version control, so relying on hand-copying during onboarding is exactly the manual, drift-prone process the team wants to avoid.
distractors.C: `CLAUDE.md` provides instructions and context to the model but does not register or launch MCP servers; listing commands there does not connect any server.
distractors.D: Environment variables can hold secrets referenced by a config, but they do not by themselves define or register MCP servers, and exporting them per-shell is not shared via version control.

scenario: You are experimenting with a brand-new, unvetted community MCP server and do not want to impose it on your teammates or risk it breaking their environments.
stem: What is the appropriate place to configure this server?

options.text: Add it to the committed project `.mcp.json` but comment it out until it is stable.
Configure it in your user-level `~/.claude.json` so it applies only to you.
Add it to `.mcp.json` and add that file to `.gitignore` so it is not committed.
Fork the repository and add the server to the fork's `.mcp.json`.

rationale.correct: User-scoped `~/.claude.json` is intended for personal and experimental servers. It applies only to you and is never shared via version control, so your teammates are unaffected while you evaluate the server.

distractors.A: JSON has no comment syntax, and even if it did, putting an experimental server in the committed team config still exposes teammates to it and pollutes the shared file.
distractors.C: Gitignoring `.mcp.json` breaks its entire purpose of sharing team tooling and would silently strip the shared servers everyone else relies on; personal experiments belong in the user scope instead.
distractors.D: Forking the repository is heavyweight and disconnected from the team's mainline; the user scope already isolates a personal server with zero repository changes.

scenario: Your shared `.mcp.json` configures a GitHub MCP server that requires a personal access token. The file is committed to a public-facing internal repository, and security has flagged that credentials must never be committed.
stem: How should the token be supplied to the server in `.mcp.json`?

options.text: Paste the literal token value into the server's `env` block so it is available at server startup.
Reference it with environment-variable expansion, e.g. `"GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"`.
Base64-encode the token before pasting it into the committed file.
Store the token in `CLAUDE.md` and instruct the agent to pass it to the server.

rationale.correct: `.mcp.json` supports environment-variable expansion such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. Committing the placeholder keeps the shared config in version control while the actual secret lives in each developer's environment and is never committed.

distractors.A: Pasting the literal token commits a live secret to version control, which is exactly the disclosure security flagged; anyone with repo access obtains the credential.
distractors.C: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; the token is trivially reversible, so a base64 blob in the committed file is still a committed secret.
distractors.D: `CLAUDE.md` is also committed and readable, so putting the token there is just another way of committing a secret, and the model cannot securely inject credentials into a server this way.

scenario: You have configured three MCP servers: a GitHub server (project scope), a Postgres server (project scope), and a personal filesystem-notes server (user scope). All three connect successfully when Claude Code starts.
stem: Which statement best describes what tools the agent can use during the session?

options.text: Only tools from one server are active at a time; you must switch servers to change which tools are available.
Only project-scoped servers' tools load; user-scoped servers require an explicit enable command per session.
Tools from all three connected servers are discovered at connection time and are available to the agent simultaneously.
The agent must be told in the prompt which single server's tools to load before it can call any of them.

rationale.correct: Tools from every configured and connected MCP server are discovered at connection time and are all available to the agent at once, regardless of whether the server is project- or user-scoped. The agent can freely choose among them within a single session.

distractors.A: There is no notion of one active server at a time; connected servers expose their tools concurrently, so no switching is required.
distractors.B: Scope determines who shares the config, not whether tools load; a successfully connected user-scoped server's tools are available just like a project-scoped server's.
distractors.D: Tool discovery is automatic at connection; the agent does not need a prompt instruction to load a server's tools before calling them.

scenario: Your custom MCP server exposes a `search_codebase` tool that uses a semantic index far more capable than plain text matching. In practice, the agent keeps reaching for the built-in `Grep` tool instead, producing weaker results.
stem: What is the most effective change to make the agent prefer your MCP tool?

options.text: Rewrite the MCP tool's description to explain its capabilities, when to use it, and what it returns.
Remove the built-in `Grep` tool from the agent's allowed tools so it has no alternative to use.
Rename the MCP tool to `grep_v2` so it sorts ahead of the built-in alphabetically.
Add a system-prompt rule that forbids the agent from ever performing code search.

rationale.correct: Agents select tools largely from their descriptions. A detailed MCP tool description that explains capabilities, appropriate use cases, and the richer output lets the agent recognize when the MCP tool beats a built-in like Grep, which is the intended way to shift preference.

distractors.B: Stripping Grep is a blunt fix that removes a legitimately useful built-in for cases the semantic tool does not cover, and it treats the symptom rather than the weak description that caused mis-selection.
distractors.C: Tool selection is driven by descriptions and relevance, not alphabetical ordering, so renaming has no reliable effect and obscures the tool's purpose.
distractors.D: A blanket prohibition on code search breaks legitimate workflows and still does not tell the agent when the MCP tool is the right instrument.

scenario: An agent working with your issue-tracker MCP server repeatedly makes many exploratory tool calls just to learn which issues, docs, and database tables exist before it can do real work, inflating latency and token use.
stem: Which MCP capability is designed to give the agent this up-front visibility and reduce the exploratory calls?

options.text: Adding more granular MCP tools, one per possible query, so each call returns less data.
Exposing content catalogs (issue summaries, doc hierarchies, schemas) as MCP resources.
Raising the agent's max iteration cap so it has enough budget to finish its exploratory calls.
Moving the server from project scope to user scope so its connection and listing calls respond faster.

rationale.correct: MCP resources expose content catalogs such as issue summaries, documentation hierarchies, and database schemas. Giving the agent this visibility up front means it no longer has to discover what exists through repeated exploratory tool calls, cutting latency and token use.

distractors.A: Proliferating fine-grained tools multiplies the number of calls needed to discover what exists; it worsens, rather than fixes, the exploratory-call problem.
distractors.C: Increasing the iteration cap just permits more of the wasteful exploration; it addresses the budget, not the missing visibility that causes the exploration.
distractors.D: Scope controls sharing of the config, not whether the agent can see a catalog of available content; changing scope does nothing to reduce exploratory calls.

scenario: Your team needs standard Jira integration for reading and updating tickets. A well-maintained community Jira MCP server already covers exactly these operations, but a colleague proposes building a bespoke server from scratch.
stem: What is the recommended approach for choosing between a community and a custom MCP server here?

options.text: Always build custom servers so the team fully controls every line of integration code.
Use the community Jira server, reserving custom servers for team-specific workflows it does not cover.
Avoid MCP entirely for Jira and instead have the agent shell out to `curl` against the Jira REST API directly.
Build a custom server only because Jira is proprietary, regardless of what community servers offer.

rationale.correct: For standard integrations like Jira, choosing a mature community MCP server avoids reinventing well-solved functionality. Custom servers should be reserved for team-specific workflows that no community server covers, which is the efficient division of effort.

distractors.A: Always building custom duplicates maintained community work, adding maintenance burden and delay for a standard integration that is already solved.
distractors.C: Dropping MCP to have the agent drive raw `curl` calls forfeits the structured tool interface, descriptions, and resources MCP provides, and is harder to secure and maintain.
distractors.D: Proprietariness alone does not justify a custom build; the deciding factor is whether a suitable community server already covers the standard operations, which here it does.

scenario: A new teammate reports that after cloning the repo, the agent cannot see the shared Postgres MCP tools that everyone else uses, even though the project `.mcp.json` is present. Their `~/.claude.json` defines an unrelated personal server that works fine.
stem: What is the most likely cause and correct diagnosis?

options.text: The project `.mcp.json` overrides the user config, so the personal server is what actually broke the Postgres connection.
The Postgres server in `.mcp.json` references an environment variable the teammate hasn't set, so it fails to connect and exposes no tools.
User-scoped servers always take priority, so the personal server suppresses all project-scoped tools until it is removed.
Project-scoped tools only appear after the teammate re-commits the `.mcp.json` file from their own machine, which registers it with their local client.

rationale.correct: The shared config is present, so scoping is fine; the likely failure is a missing credential. If `.mcp.json` references something like `${DATABASE_URL}` that the teammate has not set in their environment, the Postgres server fails to connect and its tools are never discovered, while unrelated servers keep working.

distractors.A: Project and user scopes are additive, not mutually overriding; a working personal server does not disable a project-scoped one, so this misdiagnoses the interaction.
distractors.C: There is no priority rule by which user-scoped servers suppress project-scoped tools; all connected servers expose their tools simultaneously.
distractors.D: The teammate consumes the committed `.mcp.json` as-is; re-committing an identical file from their machine changes nothing and is not how project config propagates.

scenario: You need to find every place in a large TypeScript codebase that calls the function `computeInvoiceTotal`, including callers inside deeply nested feature directories, so you can update its signature.
stem: Which built-in tool is the correct first choice for locating all call sites?

options.text: Grep, searching file contents across the codebase for the pattern `computeInvoiceTotal`.
Glob, matching a file-name pattern like `**/*invoice*.ts` to find files that might call it.
Read, opening each source file in turn and scanning it visually for the call.
Edit, attempting a no-op modification on the function name to reveal where it is used.

rationale.correct: Grep searches file contents for a pattern and is purpose-built for finding call sites, error messages, or import statements across a codebase. Searching for `computeInvoiceTotal` returns every line and file where the name appears, which is exactly the set of callers you need.

distractors.B: Glob matches file paths by name/extension pattern, not file contents. It could surface files whose names contain 'invoice', but callers can live in any file regardless of name, so it would both miss real callers and include irrelevant files.
distractors.C: Reading every file one by one to scan for a call does not scale and is the incremental-understanding anti-pattern the tools are designed to avoid; Grep answers the same question in a single pass.
distractors.D: Edit performs a targeted modification at a unique anchor; it does not search for usages and would fail or corrupt code rather than report call sites.

scenario: A reviewer asks you to open every React component test in the repository. Tests follow the convention of a `.test.tsx` suffix and are scattered across many nested feature folders.
stem: Which tool and invocation efficiently enumerates just those files?

options.text: Read the repository root directory to list its immediate children and infer where tests live.
Grep for the string `.test.tsx` inside file contents to find the test files.
Glob with the pattern `**/*.test.tsx` to match test files by path across all directories.
Write a temporary manifest file listing candidate test paths, then open each entry.

rationale.correct: Glob matches files by path/name patterns, and `**/*.test.tsx` recursively selects every file with the `.test.tsx` suffix regardless of how deeply it is nested. This is the canonical use of Glob for finding files by naming convention.

distractors.A: Reading a directory only lists that directory's entries and returns an error rather than file contents; it cannot recursively find files matching a suffix across nested folders.
distractors.B: Grep searches file contents, not file names. Searching contents for `.test.tsx` would match incidental text (imports, comments) and would not reliably enumerate the test files themselves.
distractors.D: Hand-building a manifest is unnecessary busywork; Glob already produces the exact matching path list in one call.

scenario: In `config/settings.py` you need to change a single line, `TIMEOUT = 30`, to `TIMEOUT = 60`. The string `TIMEOUT = 30` appears exactly once in the file.
stem: What is the most appropriate tool for this modification?

options.text: Write, regenerating the entire file with the new value from scratch.
Edit, replacing the unique text `TIMEOUT = 30` with `TIMEOUT = 60`.
Grep, which will update the matched line in place.
Glob, targeting the file by path and applying the change.

rationale.correct: Edit performs a targeted modification by matching unique text. Because `TIMEOUT = 30` occurs exactly once, Edit can anchor on it unambiguously and swap in the new value without touching the rest of the file, which is the safest and most precise choice.

distractors.A: Write overwrites the whole file and requires you to reproduce all other content perfectly; it is overkill and risks introducing errors when a single unique-anchor Edit suffices.
distractors.C: Grep only searches and reports matches; it is a read-only search tool and cannot modify files.
distractors.D: Glob only lists files matching a path pattern; it performs no content modification.

scenario: You want to update the second occurrence of `retries = 3` in `worker.py` to `retries = 5`, but that exact line appears in three different functions. Your Edit call fails because the anchor text is not unique.
stem: What is the recommended way to complete the change reliably?

options.text: Use Glob to disambiguate which occurrence Edit should target.
Retry the same Edit repeatedly until one of the three matches happens to be selected.
Delete the whole file with a Bash command and recreate it from memory.
Read the full file, then Write it back with only the intended occurrence changed.

rationale.correct: When Edit cannot find unique anchor text, the reliable fallback is to Read the full file to load its exact current contents, then Write it back with only the intended change applied. This guarantees you modify the correct occurrence while preserving everything else verbatim.

distractors.A: Glob only matches file paths and plays no role in disambiguating text occurrences within a single file.
distractors.B: Edit does not pick an arbitrary match when text is non-unique; retrying the identical call keeps failing and never disambiguates. Expanding the anchor with surrounding unique context (or the Read+Write fallback) is required.
distractors.C: Deleting and recreating from memory risks data loss and reproduction errors; the Read+Write fallback preserves the file's real contents.

scenario: You are new to a service and need to understand how an incoming HTTP request flows to the database. The repository has hundreds of files.
stem: Which approach best reflects building codebase understanding incrementally with the built-in tools?

options.text: Grep for an entry point such as the route registration, then Read that file and follow its imports.
Read every file in the repository from top to bottom before forming any hypothesis, so no relevant layer is missed.
Glob for `**/*.py` and open the resulting files in alphabetical order until the flow becomes clear.
Write a summary document of the expected architecture first, then search only for text that confirms it.

rationale.correct: The recommended pattern is incremental: use Grep to locate a concrete entry point (route registration, handler name), then Read that file and follow its imports to trace the flow to the next layer. You expand understanding along the actual call path rather than loading everything upfront.

distractors.B: Reading every file upfront is the exact anti-pattern the incremental approach replaces; it wastes effort and context on code unrelated to the flow you are tracing.
distractors.C: Globbing all files and opening them alphabetically ignores the dependency structure; file order is unrelated to how the request actually flows through the system.
distractors.D: Writing a summary before investigating and then searching only for confirming text invites confirmation bias and produces conclusions ungrounded in the code.

scenario: A wrapper module `api/index.ts` re-exports many symbols (e.g., `export { fetchUser, fetchOrders, fetchInvoice } from './clients'`). You must find every consumer of each re-exported name across the codebase.
stem: What is the correct sequence of tool use?

options.text: Grep once for the wrapper's path `api/index.ts` and treat every file that matches as a consumer of the module.
Read the wrapper to list its exported names, then Grep the codebase for each name to find consumers.
Glob for `**/index.ts` and assume those barrel files contain all consumers of the re-exported symbols.
Edit the wrapper to rename the exports and rely on the resulting build failures to reveal each consumer.

rationale.correct: To trace usage across a wrapper module you first Read the wrapper to identify all exported names, then Grep the codebase for each name individually. Consumers import the underlying symbols by name, so per-name content searches reveal the full set of call sites the wrapper path alone would hide.

distractors.A: Searching for the file path finds only the wrapper file (and imports of the module), not consumers that reference the individual re-exported symbols; it undercounts usage.
distractors.C: Glob for `index.ts` files matches unrelated barrel files by name and tells you nothing about where the specific symbols are consumed.
distractors.D: Renaming exports to break the build is a destructive, unreliable discovery method; a read-then-grep search enumerates consumers without modifying code.

scenario: Production logs show the message `Payment gateway timeout exceeded`. You want to jump straight to the code that emits it, but you do not know which file it lives in.
stem: Which tool most directly gets you there?

options.text: Write a new logging statement near the payment calls and redeploy to locate the source at runtime.
Glob for files named `*payment*` and open each match to look for the message text.
Read the project's top-level README to find where this error and its source module are documented.
Grep file contents for the literal error string `Payment gateway timeout exceeded`.

rationale.correct: Grep searches file contents for patterns such as error messages. Searching for the literal string `Payment gateway timeout exceeded` lands directly on the line that emits it, regardless of which file it is in, which is the fastest path from a log message to its source.

distractors.A: Adding a log statement and redeploying is a slow, invasive way to find code that a single content search already pinpoints.
distractors.B: Glob matches file names, not contents; the emitting code may live in a file whose name has nothing to do with 'payment', so this both misses the target and adds noise.
distractors.C: A README rarely contains exact runtime strings and would not point to the emitting line; content search is the direct route.

scenario: You must replace a repeated boilerplate license header that appears verbatim at the top of dozens of files, and additionally the exact header text also recurs inside one file's embedded documentation string.
stem: For the single file where the header text is not unique, which tactic correctly applies the update?

options.text: Skip the file entirely, because non-unique anchor text means Edit cannot target the header safely.
Run Edit with `replace_all` so every occurrence of the header in that file is changed in a single call.
Read that file in full and Write it back with only the top-of-file header replaced.
Grep for the header text and let the search tool overwrite the first match it finds in the file.

rationale.correct: When the anchor text is not unique within a file and you must change only one specific occurrence, the reliable fallback is Read the full file then Write it back with just the top-of-file header replaced. This preserves the embedded duplicate that should stay unchanged.

distractors.A: Even if the header text alone is not a unique Edit anchor, the file can still be updated safely: the Read+Write fallback exists precisely for this case, so skipping the file is unnecessary and leaves it with the old header.
distractors.B: `replace_all` would also rewrite the embedded documentation copy that must remain unchanged, causing an unintended modification; it is wrong when only one of several occurrences should change.
distractors.D: Grep is read-only and cannot overwrite matches; it neither modifies files nor targets a specific occurrence.

scenario: A senior engineer added detailed commit-message and testing conventions that Claude Code follows perfectly on her machine. A newly onboarded teammate clones the same repository, but Claude Code ignores those conventions entirely for him. The engineer confirms the guidance lives in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
stem: What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: The repository was cloned before the file was committed; the teammate should `git pull` to receive the `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file.
User-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is not shared via version control; move the conventions into the project-level `CLAUDE.md`.
Directory-level CLAUDE.md files always override user-level ones, so the teammate must delete his subdirectory CLAUDE.md files.
The teammate needs to run `/memory reset` to force his session to re-read the user-level configuration from the repository.

rationale.correct: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level (personal) configuration that lives in the individual's home directory. It is never committed to the repository, so a teammate's clone will never contain it. Instructions meant to be shared across a team belong in project-level configuration (root `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`), which is version-controlled and loaded for anyone who checks out the repo.

distractors.A: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` lives in the user's home directory, not the repository, so it is never part of the git history and cannot be received by pulling.
distractors.C: Directory-level files add scope for their subtree; they do not explain why a project-wide convention is missing, and deleting them does nothing to distribute the engineer's personal file.
distractors.D: `/memory` is a diagnostic that lists loaded files; it cannot import a file that does not exist on the teammate's machine, and there is no such reset behavior that pulls another user's home-directory config.

scenario: A monorepo has a root `CLAUDE.md` stating "use 4-space indentation," and a `services/payments/CLAUDE.md` stating "payments code uses 2-space indentation and requires an audit-log entry for every mutation." A developer opens Claude Code and edits a file inside `services/payments/`.
stem: Which instructions are in effect for that edit?

options.text: Only the root `CLAUDE.md`, because root configuration always takes precedence over subdirectory files.
Only the `services/payments/CLAUDE.md`, because a directory-level file completely replaces all higher-level configuration.
Neither, until the developer manually imports both files with `@import` at the top of the edited file.
Both files apply, with the more specific `services/payments/CLAUDE.md` rules taking precedence where they conflict with the root.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md files are hierarchical and additive: the project root provides the baseline, and directory-level files for the path being worked in layer on additional, more specific context. Where the more specific file conflicts with a broader one, the more specific (closer to the file) guidance wins, so payments code gets 2-space indentation plus the audit-log requirement while still inheriting non-conflicting root rules.

distractors.A: Precedence runs from general to specific; the root does not override a directory-level file that is closer to the edited file.
distractors.B: Directory-level files supplement rather than wholesale replace the hierarchy; non-conflicting root guidance still applies.
distractors.C: The hierarchy loads automatically based on the file's location; `@import` is for pulling in external files, not for activating directory-level CLAUDE.md files.

scenario: A platform team maintains a shared `docs/standards/` folder containing `security.md`, `logging.md`, and `graphql.md`. Each package in the monorepo should follow only the standards relevant to it, and the team wants each package's `CLAUDE.md` to stay short and to automatically reflect updates to the shared standards files.
stem: What is the recommended way to wire the relevant standards into each package's `CLAUDE.md`?

options.text: Use `@import` (e.g., `@docs/standards/security.md`) in each package's `CLAUDE.md` for just the standards that package needs.
Copy-paste the full text of every standards file into every package's `CLAUDE.md` so the guidance is guaranteed to be present.
Add all three standards files to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so they load globally for every package in the monorepo.
Rename the standards files to `CLAUDE.md` and place a copy in each relevant package directory so they load by path.

rationale.correct: The `@import` syntax lets a `CLAUDE.md` reference external files, keeping it modular. Each package maintainer imports only the standards relevant to that package's domain, and because the imports point at the single source-of-truth files, edits to those standards propagate everywhere they are imported without duplication.

distractors.B: Copy-pasting duplicates content, bloats each file, and guarantees drift the moment a standard is updated in one place but not the copies.
distractors.C: User-level config is personal and not shared via version control, so teammates would not receive it; it also cannot express per-package selectivity.
distractors.D: Renaming and copying still duplicates the content and loses the single-source-of-truth benefit that `@import` provides.

scenario: A project's root `CLAUDE.md` has grown to 900 lines covering testing, API conventions, and deployment. Contributors complain it is hard to navigate and that unrelated sections make it hard to see what applies to a given task.
stem: Which restructuring best addresses this while keeping the guidance version-controlled and shared?

options.text: Move the entire file to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so it is out of the repository and only loaded when needed.
Delete the least-used sections to shrink the file below 300 lines, keeping just the guidance contributors reference most.
Split the monolith into focused, committed topic files under `.claude/rules/` (e.g., `testing.md`, `deployment.md`).
Put each topic in a separate directory-level `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root (e.g., three CLAUDE.md files side by side).

rationale.correct: The `.claude/rules/` directory is the recommended alternative to a monolithic `CLAUDE.md`: topic-specific files like `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`, and `deployment.md` keep each concern focused and easy to maintain while remaining committed, version-controlled project configuration shared with the whole team.

distractors.A: Moving guidance to user-level config removes it from version control, so teammates lose it entirely; this trades an organization problem for a sharing failure.
distractors.B: Deleting content loses guidance rather than organizing it, and does nothing to make the remaining content easier to navigate by topic.
distractors.D: You cannot have multiple `CLAUDE.md` files in the same directory, and directory-level files are for scoping by path, not for organizing topics that all apply project-wide.

scenario: A developer notices Claude Code behaves inconsistently across sessions: sometimes it follows a naming convention and sometimes it does not. She suspects a configuration file is not being loaded but is unsure which files are actually in effect.
stem: What is the most direct way to diagnose which memory/configuration files are currently loaded?

options.text: Run `git log` on the `CLAUDE.md` files to confirm they were committed and haven't been reverted recently.
Run the `/memory` command, which lists the memory files currently loaded in her session.
Restart Claude Code repeatedly until the convention is followed, so the configuration files get re-read.
Add the convention to every file in the repository so at least one copy is guaranteed to load.

rationale.correct: The `/memory` command shows exactly which memory files (user-level, project-level, directory-level, and imported files) are loaded in the current session, so she can verify whether the expected CLAUDE.md and imported files are in effect — making it the direct tool for diagnosing why guidance is or is not taking effect and catching a file that silently failed to load.

distractors.A: `git log` confirms a file was committed but says nothing about whether the current session actually loaded it, which is the real question.
distractors.C: Restarting is guesswork that provides no visibility into which files are loaded and does not identify the missing configuration.
distractors.D: Blanketing the repo with duplicated instructions is an anti-pattern that causes drift and still does not tell her which files load.

scenario: An engineer has a personal preference to always receive terse, bullet-point explanations from Claude Code, but this preference should not be imposed on teammates who share the same repositories.
stem: Where should she place this instruction?

options.text: In her user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which applies to her across all her projects.
In the project's root `CLAUDE.md`, which is committed and shared with the whole team.
In a `.claude/rules/style.md` file committed to each repository, so the style rule stays separate from project docs.
In a directory-level `CLAUDE.md` in the repository's `src/` folder, where most of her work happens.

rationale.correct: User-level configuration (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) applies only to that user and is not shared via version control, making it the correct home for personal preferences that should follow the engineer across all her projects without affecting teammates.

distractors.B: Root `CLAUDE.md` is committed and shared, so it would impose her personal style on every teammate, which is explicitly what she wants to avoid.
distractors.C: A committed `.claude/rules/` file is shared with the team, so it would affect everyone working in that repository.
distractors.D: A directory-level `CLAUDE.md` is still committed and shared; it also scopes by path, which is unrelated to a personal, cross-project preference.

scenario: A team wants shared coding standards to load automatically for everyone, personal shortcuts to load only for the individual, and infrastructure-as-code rules to apply only when working inside the `terraform/` directory.
stem: Which placement correctly satisfies all three requirements?

options.text: Put all three in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the hierarchy will work out who each one applies to and in which directories.
Put all three in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`; user-level config cascades down into every teammate's project automatically.
Put shared standards in a directory-level `terraform/CLAUDE.md`, personal shortcuts in the root `CLAUDE.md`, and infrastructure rules in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
Shared standards in the committed root `CLAUDE.md`, personal shortcuts in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and infrastructure rules in `terraform/CLAUDE.md`.

rationale.correct: Each requirement maps to the layer whose scope matches it: team-wide standards belong in the committed project-level root `CLAUDE.md`; personal shortcuts belong in the user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (personal, not shared); and directory-scoped infrastructure rules belong in a directory-level `terraform/CLAUDE.md` that loads only when working in that subtree.

distractors.A: Putting personal shortcuts in the committed root file would share them with everyone, and root guidance is not automatically scoped to only the `terraform/` directory.
distractors.B: User-level config is personal and never distributed via version control, so teammates would receive none of it.
distractors.C: This inverts every mapping: shared standards would be limited to `terraform/`, personal shortcuts would be shared with the team via the root file, and infrastructure rules placed at user-level would not be shared and would not be path-scoped.
