scenario: A `packages/api/CLAUDE.md` contains the line `@../../docs/standards/graphql.md`. A reviewer argues this import is pointless and that the same effect could be achieved by simply pasting the GraphQL standards into the file.
stem: What is the strongest justification for keeping the `@import` rather than pasting the content?

options.text: Imports make Claude Code load files faster than inline text of the same length, which keeps session startup quick.
Only imported files count toward the hierarchy; inline text in a CLAUDE.md is ignored by Claude Code.
`@import` keeps the standard single-sourced, so updates to the canonical GraphQL file propagate to every importing package.
Pasting content is forbidden by the CLAUDE.md schema, so imports are the only mechanism the tool accepts for standards.

rationale.correct: The value of `@import` is modularity and single-sourcing: the GraphQL standard is authored once in a canonical file and referenced by every package that needs it. When the standard changes, every importing package reflects the update automatically, eliminating the duplication and drift that pasting would introduce, while each package's CLAUDE.md stays short and focused on what is relevant to it.

distractors.A: Load performance is not the rationale; the benefit is maintainability and avoiding duplicated, drifting copies.
distractors.B: Inline instructions in a CLAUDE.md are absolutely honored; `@import` is a convenience for referencing external files, not a requirement for content to count.
distractors.D: There is no rule forbidding inline content; CLAUDE.md files routinely contain inline instructions, so this is fabricated.

scenario: Your team maintains a standard code review checklist. You want to package it as a custom `/review` slash command that is automatically available to every developer the moment they clone or pull the repository.
stem: Where should you create the command definition file so it ships with the repo and requires no per-developer setup?

options.text: In the project's `.claude/commands/` directory, committed to version control.
In each developer's `~/.claude/commands/` directory in their home folder.
In the project root `CLAUDE.md` file as a section describing the review steps.
In a `.claude/config.json` file under a `commands` array.

rationale.correct: Project-scoped slash commands live in the repository's `.claude/commands/` directory. Because that directory is committed to version control, the command travels with the repo and becomes available to everyone who clones or pulls it, with no manual per-developer installation.

distractors.B: `~/.claude/commands/` is the user (personal) scope. Commands there exist only on one developer's machine and are never shared via the repository, so teammates would not receive the `/review` command.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded project context and instructions, not invocable slash-command definitions. Describing the steps there does not create a `/review` command.
distractors.D: There is no `.claude/config.json` `commands` array mechanism in Claude Code; commands are defined as files in a `commands/` directory, not registered in a config array.

scenario: A developer has a personal `/scratch` command that scaffolds throwaway experiment files the way she likes them. It reflects her individual workflow and would only add noise for the rest of the team.
stem: Where should she place this command so it is available in all her projects but never committed or imposed on teammates?

options.text: In the project's `.claude/commands/` directory so it is version-controlled.
In `~/.claude/commands/` in her home directory (user scope).
In a `.claude/skills/` SKILL.md file with `context: fork` set.
In the project CLAUDE.md so it loads automatically for the session.

rationale.correct: User-scoped commands belong in `~/.claude/commands/`. They live in the developer's home directory, are available across all her projects, and are never committed to any repository, so teammates are unaffected.

distractors.A: Putting it in the project's `.claude/commands/` would commit the command to version control and push it onto everyone who pulls the repo, the opposite of the personal, non-shared intent.
distractors.C: A skill is a different construct from a slash command, and `context: fork` controls context isolation, not scope or sharing; this neither makes it personal nor keeps it out of the repo if placed in the project tree.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.md stores project context, not slash commands, and a project CLAUDE.md is typically shared via the repo, so it would not give a private, cross-project personal command.

scenario: You are building a `codebase-audit` skill that scans the whole repo and emits a very long report. When invoked in normal sessions, its verbose output floods the main conversation and pushes out context you still need for the actual task.
stem: Which SKILL.md frontmatter setting keeps the skill's verbose output from polluting the main conversation?

options.text: `allowed-tools` restricting the skill to read-only tools.
`argument-hint` prompting for the directory to scan.
`context: fork`, which runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context.
`disable-model-invocation: true` so the skill only runs manually.

rationale.correct: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context. The skill does its work and verbose output in the fork, and only a concise result returns to the main session, so the lengthy report never pollutes the primary conversation's context.

distractors.A: `allowed-tools` restricts which tools the skill may call; it limits capability, not the volume of output that returns to the main conversation, so verbose text would still flood the session.
distractors.B: `argument-hint` only prompts the developer for parameters at invocation time; it has no effect on where the skill's output lands or on context isolation.
distractors.D: Controlling whether the model can auto-invoke the skill does not isolate its context; when the skill does run, its verbose output would still land in the main conversation.

scenario: You are authoring a `format-fixtures` skill that should only ever write and edit files. You want to guarantee that, while the skill runs, Claude cannot execute shell commands or perform other destructive actions even if the model would otherwise reach for them.
stem: Which SKILL.md frontmatter field enforces that restriction?

options.text: `context: fork`, isolating the skill in a sub-agent.
`argument-hint`, listing the parameters the skill accepts.
`model`, pinning the skill to a smaller model with fewer tools.
`allowed-tools`, whitelisting only the file write/edit tools.

rationale.correct: `allowed-tools` in the skill frontmatter whitelists exactly which tools the skill may use during execution. Restricting it to file write/edit tools prevents Claude from running shell commands or other destructive operations while the skill runs.

distractors.A: `context: fork` isolates the skill's context from the main conversation but does not by itself narrow which tools the skill is permitted to call.
distractors.B: `argument-hint` only prompts the developer for parameters; it places no constraint on tool access or destructive actions.
distractors.C: Choosing a model does not define a tool permission boundary; the available tools are governed by `allowed-tools`, not by which model is selected.

scenario: Your `new-service` skill needs a service name and a target directory to work. Teammates keep invoking it with no arguments and are unsure what to supply, so it stalls waiting for input.
stem: Which SKILL.md frontmatter field is designed to tell developers what parameters to provide when they invoke the skill?

options.text: `argument-hint`, which prompts for the expected parameters at invocation.
`allowed-tools`, which documents the tools by way of hinting inputs.
`context: fork`, which surfaces a parameter prompt in the sub-agent.
`description`, whose text is parsed to auto-fill missing arguments.

rationale.correct: `argument-hint` is exactly for this: it prompts developers for the required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments, making the expected inputs (e.g., service name, target directory) explicit.

distractors.B: `allowed-tools` restricts which tools the skill may call; it says nothing to the user about what arguments to pass.
distractors.C: `context: fork` controls context isolation in a sub-agent; it does not present an argument prompt or communicate expected parameters.
distractors.D: `description` helps the model decide when the skill is relevant; it is not parsed to fill in missing arguments, so it would not guide invocation parameters.

scenario: Two team needs are on the table. First, a universal coding standard (naming, error handling) that should apply to essentially every interaction. Second, a specialized, multi-step release-notes generation workflow that is only relevant occasionally, when someone is cutting a release.
stem: How should you place each so context is used efficiently?

options.text: Put both the coding standard and the release workflow in CLAUDE.md so nothing is ever missed.
Put the coding standard in CLAUDE.md (always loaded) and the release workflow in a skill (on demand).
Put both in skills so neither consumes context until invoked, keeping the baseline context lean.
Put the coding standard in a skill and the release workflow in CLAUDE.md so the release steps are always ready.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded context, ideal for universal standards that should apply to every interaction. Skills are invoked on demand, ideal for task-specific workflows that are only occasionally relevant. Matching each need to the right mechanism keeps always-loaded context lean while still making the release workflow available when needed.

distractors.A: Loading the occasional release workflow into always-loaded CLAUDE.md wastes context on every interaction for a task that is rarely relevant.
distractors.C: Making the universal coding standard an on-demand skill means it would not reliably apply to every interaction, defeating the purpose of a universal standard.
distractors.D: This inverts the correct mapping: the universal standard should be always-loaded (CLAUDE.md) and the occasional workflow should be on-demand (skill).

scenario: Your repo ships a shared `deploy` skill in `.claude/skills/deploy/`. You want your own tweaked version with extra safety checks for local experimentation, without changing the team's skill or forcing your variant on teammates.
stem: What is the recommended way to create your personal variant?

options.text: Edit the project's `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` directly and just avoid committing it.
Add `context: fork` to the shared skill so your changes stay isolated from the team.
Create a personal skill under `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name (e.g., `deploy-safe`).
Rename the shared skill in the repo to `deploy-safe` so both versions can coexist.

rationale.correct: Personal skill customization is done by creating a variant in `~/.claude/skills/` (user scope) with a different name, such as `deploy-safe`. It lives only on your machine, does not touch the shared project skill, and cannot affect teammates.

distractors.A: Editing the committed project skill and relying on not committing is error-prone: the change risks being staged or clobbering the shared version, and it does not give a cleanly separate personal variant.
distractors.B: `context: fork` isolates a skill's runtime context, not its ownership or scope; adding it to the shared skill still modifies the team's file and does not create a personal variant.
distractors.D: Renaming the shared skill inside the repo changes it for everyone who pulls the repo, which is exactly the team impact you wanted to avoid.

scenario: A teammate insists the fastest way to give everyone a shared `/deploy` slash command is to add a `commands` array to a `.claude/config.json` file, and points to CLAUDE.md as an alternative place to define it.
stem: What is the correct assessment of these two proposals?

options.text: The `.claude/config.json` `commands` array is correct; CLAUDE.md is a valid fallback.
Both are valid ways to share a command; use whichever the team prefers to maintain in version control.
CLAUDE.md is correct for defining commands; `.claude/config.json` is only for settings.
Neither: shared commands are files in the project's `.claude/commands/` directory.

rationale.correct: Shared slash commands are defined as files in the project's `.claude/commands/` directory (committed to version control). There is no `.claude/config.json` `commands` array mechanism, and CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded project context, not command definitions.

distractors.A: The `.claude/config.json` `commands` array does not exist in Claude Code, and CLAUDE.md does not define invocable commands, so this is wrong on both counts.
distractors.B: Neither approach actually creates a slash command, so 'both are valid' is incorrect.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md holds project instructions and context, not command definitions; it cannot be used to define a `/deploy` slash command.

scenario: Your codebase has distinct areas with different conventions: React components use functional style with hooks, API handlers use async/await error handling, and database models follow a repository pattern. Test files live alongside the code they test (e.g., `Button.test.tsx` next to `Button.tsx`) and are scattered across dozens of directories. You want Claude to automatically apply the same test conventions to every test file regardless of where it lives.
stem: What is the most maintainable way to ensure Claude automatically applies the correct test conventions when generating code?

options.text: Create a `.claude/rules/` file with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` so test conventions load whenever a matching file is edited.
Consolidate every area's conventions under headers in the root CLAUDE.md and rely on Claude to infer which section applies to the file it is editing.
Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each directory that contains test files, repeating the test conventions in every one.
Create a skill in `.claude/skills/` holding the test conventions and ask developers to invoke it before editing any test file.

rationale.correct: A `.claude/rules/` file with a glob `paths` pattern like `**/*.test.tsx` matches files by type across every directory, so the conventions load deterministically and automatically whenever a matching file is edited. This is exactly the case (Sample Question 6) where glob path-rules beat directory-bound CLAUDE.md files for conventions that span scattered files.

distractors.B: A single root CLAUDE.md relies on Claude inferring which header section applies rather than explicit path matching, which is unreliable and loads every area's conventions into context whether relevant or not.
distractors.C: Per-directory CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound; with test files spread across dozens of folders you would duplicate the conventions everywhere and any change would have to be made in many places, defeating maintainability.
distractors.D: Skills require manual invocation (or Claude choosing to load them), which contradicts the requirement for automatic, path-triggered application based on the file being edited.

scenario: A teammate wrote a rule that should only apply when editing Terraform configuration, but it is loading into context on every file including unrelated TypeScript components.
stem: Which YAML frontmatter field, and value form, in the `.claude/rules/` file makes the rule load only when Terraform files are being edited?

options.text: A `tags` field listing `terraform`, which Claude matches against the language of the file being edited.
A `paths` field with a glob such as `paths: ["terraform/**/*"]`, scoping the rule to matching files.
A `directory` field set to `terraform`, which limits the rule to files inside that one folder.
An `enabled: false` field that developers toggle on manually when they open Terraform files.

rationale.correct: Conditional activation is driven by a `paths` field in the rule's YAML frontmatter containing glob patterns (e.g., `terraform/**/*`). The rule loads only when the file being edited matches a pattern, keeping unrelated context out of the window.

distractors.A: There is no `tags`-based language-matching mechanism for rule activation; scoping is done with glob path patterns in the `paths` field.
distractors.C: A `directory` field is not the mechanism; `paths` accepts globs that can match a single directory or span many, and `terraform/**/*` already covers nested folders which a single-directory field would not.
distractors.D: Path-scoped rules load automatically on matching files; a manual `enabled` toggle would defeat the purpose of conditional, path-triggered activation.

scenario: Your team is deciding how to document conventions for files of a specific type (all `*.test.ts` files) that are deliberately colocated next to the source they test and therefore spread across the entire repository.
stem: Why are glob-pattern path rules in `.claude/rules/` preferable to a subdirectory CLAUDE.md for this situation?

options.text: CLAUDE.md files cannot contain conventions about testing, only project overviews and build commands for the repository.
Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load faster but cannot be version-controlled, whereas rule files are committed with the repo.
CLAUDE.md is directory-bound and would need duplicating across folders, while one `**/*.test.ts` glob rule matches every test file.
Glob rules disable the root CLAUDE.md entirely, guaranteeing no conflicting conventions are ever loaded alongside them.

rationale.correct: The core advantage is that glob patterns match files by type regardless of location, so a single rule covers test files everywhere. A CLAUDE.md is tied to the directory it sits in, so scattered files would force you to duplicate it across many folders.

distractors.A: CLAUDE.md can absolutely hold testing conventions; the issue is scope and location, not content type.
distractors.B: Both CLAUDE.md files and rule files are ordinary version-controlled files; load speed and version control are not the distinguishing factors.
distractors.D: Path rules layer with CLAUDE.md rather than disabling it; they do not switch off the root CLAUDE.md.

scenario: A large monorepo has grown to include rules for Terraform, Python services, React components, and SQL migrations. Engineers complain that Claude's context fills up with convention text that is irrelevant to the file currently being edited, increasing token usage.
stem: How does path-scoping rules with `paths` glob patterns address this complaint?

options.text: It compresses all rules into a summary that is always loaded, reducing their total size in the context window.
It loads just the rules whose globs match the file being edited, keeping irrelevant conventions out of context.
It moves rule content to a remote server that Claude queries on demand, so nothing counts against the context window.
It caps the number of rules Claude may read to the three most recently modified rule files, limiting context growth.

rationale.correct: Path-scoped rules load conditionally: only rules whose `paths` globs match the current file are pulled into context. Rules for file types you are not editing are never loaded, which keeps irrelevant conventions out of context and reduces token consumption.

distractors.A: There is no always-loaded compressed summary; the mechanism is conditional loading by path match, not summarization.
distractors.C: Rules are local repository files, not remote content queried on demand; scoping controls when they load, it does not offload them off-window.
distractors.D: There is no recency cap of three files; relevance is determined by glob path matching, not modification time.

scenario: You need Claude to apply strict SQL migration conventions, but only to migration files, which by team standard are named like `V2__add_users.sql` and live under any `*/migrations/` folder anywhere in the repo.
stem: Which `paths` value in the rule's frontmatter correctly scopes it to those migration files across all directories?

options.text: `paths: ["migrations/"]` — matches only the top-level migrations folder and its files.
`paths: ["*.sql"]` — matches every SQL file in the repository root only.
`paths: ["**/migrations/**/*.sql"]` — SQL files in any migrations folder at any depth.
`paths: ["src/db/migrations.sql"]` — matches one specific migration file path.

rationale.correct: `**/migrations/**/*.sql` uses `**` to match any depth on both sides, so it captures `*.sql` files inside a `migrations` directory located anywhere in the repository, which is exactly the cross-directory scoping required.

distractors.A: `migrations/` only refers to a single top-level folder and does not use globs to reach nested migration directories elsewhere in the repo.
distractors.B: `*.sql` (single star, no `**`) matches SQL files only at the root level and would miss migrations nested in subdirectories, while also catching non-migration SQL.
distractors.D: A single explicit file path matches exactly one file and cannot cover migration files spread across many directories.

scenario: A developer argues the team should just add a CLAUDE.md in each of the 40 directories that happen to contain test files, rather than write a path rule, because 'CLAUDE.md is the standard place for conventions.'
stem: What is the strongest reason to reject the per-directory CLAUDE.md approach for these scattered test files?

options.text: Per-directory files duplicate the conventions across 40 places and new test directories silently miss them; one glob rule covers all.
CLAUDE.md files are ignored by Claude Code unless placed at the repository root, so subdirectory copies would not be picked up.
Path rules run faster because they are compiled once at startup, while CLAUDE.md is interpreted at runtime per request.
Per-directory CLAUDE.md files require an admin permission that ordinary developers cannot grant.

rationale.correct: The maintainability problem is duplication and drift: directory-bound CLAUDE.md files copied into 40 directories must be updated in 40 places, and any new test directory silently misses them. A single glob-scoped rule (`**/*.test.tsx`) matches the file type everywhere automatically with one source of truth.

distractors.B: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are honored, not ignored; the objection is about scope and duplication, not that they fail to load.
distractors.C: There is no compiled-versus-interpreted performance distinction between rules and CLAUDE.md; that is a fabricated advantage.
distractors.D: No special admin permission is required to add a CLAUDE.md; that is not a real constraint.

scenario: Your repo has a rule at `.claude/rules/react-components.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.tsx"]` and another at `.claude/rules/tests.md` with `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`. A developer opens `Card.test.tsx` to edit it.
stem: Which rule(s) will Claude load into context for this file, and why?

options.text: Only `react-components.md`, because `.tsx` extension rules take precedence over test-file rules.
Both rules, because `Card.test.tsx` matches both the `**/*.tsx` and `**/*.test.tsx` glob patterns.
Neither rule, because a file cannot match two path patterns at once, so the conflict cancels both.
Only `tests.md`, because the more specific pattern always suppresses broader patterns that also match.

rationale.correct: Glob matching is independent per rule: `Card.test.tsx` ends in `.tsx` (matching `**/*.tsx`) and also ends in `.test.tsx` (matching `**/*.test.tsx`), so both rules activate and both sets of conventions load. Overlapping globs stack rather than override.

distractors.A: There is no `.tsx`-over-test precedence rule; matching is evaluated per pattern, so the component rule does not exclude the test rule.
distractors.C: A single file can match multiple glob patterns simultaneously; matching is not mutually exclusive.
distractors.D: Specificity does not cause one matching rule to suppress another; both matching rules load together.

scenario: An architect wants conventions for infrastructure-as-code to apply the moment anyone edits a Terraform file, no matter which service subdirectory it lives in, without engineers having to remember to trigger anything.
stem: Which combination of mechanism and configuration best satisfies both the 'automatic' and 'spans directories' requirements?

options.text: A `.claude/rules/` file with `paths: ["**/*.tf"]`, activating automatically on Terraform files anywhere in the tree.
A slash command `/terraform-conventions` that engineers run before editing infrastructure files to load the conventions.
A skill in `.claude/skills/` that Claude may choose to load when it thinks the task is Terraform-related.
A single CLAUDE.md in the top-level `terraform/` directory describing the conventions for infrastructure code.

rationale.correct: A rule with glob `paths: ["**/*.tf"]` activates automatically whenever a matching file is edited and, because of the `**` prefix, matches Terraform files in any service subdirectory. That satisfies both the automatic and cross-directory requirements.

distractors.B: A slash command must be manually invoked, so it fails the 'without remembering to trigger anything' requirement.
distractors.C: A skill is loaded at Claude's discretion or by invocation, which is non-deterministic and not automatically tied to the file path being edited.
distractors.D: A single top-level `terraform/` CLAUDE.md is directory-bound and would not cover Terraform files that live under other service subdirectories.

scenario: You are asked to restructure a monolithic application into microservices. The work spans dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies before any code moves.
stem: Which approach best fits this task?

options.text: Enter plan mode to explore the codebase, map dependencies, and design an implementation approach before making any changes.
Start in direct execution and let the implementation reveal the natural service boundaries as you go.
Use direct execution with comprehensive upfront instructions detailing exactly how each service should be structured.
Begin in direct execution and switch to plan mode only if you hit unexpected complexity mid-implementation.

rationale.correct: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions—exactly what monolith-to-microservices restructuring requires. It enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework.

distractors.B: Letting implementation reveal boundaries risks discovering dependencies late, after changes are already entangled, which is the costly rework plan mode exists to prevent.
distractors.C: Comprehensive upfront instructions assume you already know the correct structure without exploring the code; the architectural decisions still need discovery, which is what plan mode provides.
distractors.D: The complexity is already stated in the requirements (dozens of files, service-boundary and dependency decisions), not something that might emerge later, so plan mode is warranted from the start.

scenario: A user reports a crash. The stack trace points to one function that dereferences a possibly-null config value, and the fix is a single guard clause in that one file.
stem: What is the most appropriate way to make this change?

options.text: Enter plan mode first to document a design before touching the function.
Use direct execution to add the guard clause, since the scope is clear and confined to one function.
Delegate the whole fix to the Explore subagent so it can search the codebase before editing.
Enter plan mode because any code change involving null handling is inherently architectural.

rationale.correct: Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes such as a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace. The problem, location, and fix are all known, so plan mode's exploration-before-committing value does not apply.

distractors.A: Plan mode adds overhead without benefit here; there is nothing to explore or design when the stack trace already pinpoints the one-line fix.
distractors.C: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery; a one-function fix with a known location needs no discovery phase, so delegating it is over-engineering.
distractors.D: A localized null guard is not an architectural decision; treating every change as architectural defeats the purpose of matching mode to complexity.

scenario: You are planning a large migration and need to understand how an unfamiliar 200-file legacy module wires together. Fully reading and grepping it in the main conversation would flood the context window with file dumps and search output, leaving little room for the actual planning.
stem: What is the best way to run this discovery phase?

options.text: Read and grep every file directly in the main conversation so all the details stay available for the planning that follows.
Skip discovery and start editing, relying on tests to surface how the module is wired.
Use the Explore subagent for the verbose discovery and have it return a concise summary to the main conversation.
Raise the model's context window setting so the contents of all 200 files fit in one conversation at once.

rationale.correct: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns a summary to the main conversation, preventing context-window exhaustion during multi-phase tasks so the planning that follows retains the room it needs.

distractors.A: Reading and grepping everything in the main conversation is exactly the context flooding to avoid; the raw output crowds out the planning work.
distractors.B: Skipping discovery on an unfamiliar 200-file module invites the costly late-dependency surprises that up-front exploration is meant to prevent.
distractors.D: A larger context window does not solve attention dilution or the crowding of planning by raw dumps; isolating discovery in a subagent is the intended structural fix.

scenario: Your team must migrate from a deprecated HTTP client library to a new one. Preliminary search shows the old library is imported in 45+ files with several call patterns, and the new library changes both the request API and the error-handling model.
stem: Which approach should you take before changing code?

options.text: Enter plan mode to survey the usage patterns and design a migration approach before editing.
Fix the first file that fails to compile and repeat file by file until the build passes.
Use direct execution because a library swap is a mechanical find-and-replace regardless of file count.
Skip planning and rely on a global search-and-replace of the old import path.

rationale.correct: A migration affecting 45+ files with changed request and error-handling APIs is a large-scale, multi-file change with real design implications—precisely the profile plan mode targets. Exploring usage patterns first lets you design a consistent approach and avoid costly rework.

distractors.B: Fixing file by file as the build breaks is reactive; it discovers the differing call and error patterns too late and produces inconsistent conversions across the 45+ files.
distractors.C: The change is not mechanical: the new library alters the request API and error model, so a blind replace would break behavior; scale plus semantic change is what makes it plan-worthy.
distractors.D: A global import replace ignores the differing call patterns and the new error-handling model, guaranteeing broken call sites that up-front planning would have caught.

scenario: You used plan mode to investigate the library migration from the previous scenario and Claude produced a clear, ordered migration plan you have reviewed and approved. Each remaining step is now well-defined and low-ambiguity.
stem: What is the most effective way to carry out the approved plan?

options.text: Stay in plan mode for the entire migration so every edit is re-planned before it is applied.
Discard the plan and start over in direct execution, working from the code rather than from the plan.
Re-run the Explore subagent before each step to re-derive the plan from the current state of the code.
Switch to direct execution for the now well-scoped steps, using plan mode's output as the guide.

rationale.correct: A recommended pattern is combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation: once planning has resolved the ambiguity and the steps are well-scoped, direct execution carries them out efficiently while the approved plan guides the work.

distractors.A: Re-planning every edit after the design is settled adds overhead with no benefit; plan mode's value was in the investigation, which is already done.
distractors.B: Discarding the approved plan throws away the exploration you paid for and reintroduces the risk of inconsistent, unguided changes.
distractors.C: Rerunning Explore to re-derive the plan repeats completed discovery work; the summary and plan already exist and only need executing.

scenario: You need to add real-time notifications to an app. There are several viable integrations—server-sent events, WebSockets, and a third-party push service—each with different infrastructure requirements and operational trade-offs, and the team has not decided which to adopt.
stem: How should you proceed?

options.text: Pick WebSockets immediately in direct execution because it is the most common choice for real-time features.
Enter plan mode to explore the codebase and compare the approaches' infrastructure trade-offs before committing.
Implement all three approaches directly and keep whichever works best.
Use direct execution and defer the infrastructure decision until after the feature is coded.

rationale.correct: When there are multiple valid approaches with different infrastructure requirements and no chosen direction, plan mode fits: it enables exploring the codebase and weighing the design trade-offs before committing, which is where the real risk lies.

distractors.A: Defaulting to the popular option skips the trade-off analysis the situation demands; the differing infrastructure requirements make the choice non-obvious.
distractors.C: Building all three is wasteful and still leaves the decision unmade; plan mode compares approaches without paying to implement each.
distractors.D: Deferring an infrastructure decision until after coding invites rework because the chosen approach shapes the code that would already be written.

scenario: A teammate argues that for a known architectural refactor spanning many files, the team should always begin in direct execution and only enter plan mode if the work turns out to be unexpectedly complex.
stem: What is the strongest objection to this policy?

options.text: Plan mode cannot be entered once any edits have been made in a session, so switching later is impossible.
The complexity is stated in the requirements rather than emerging later, so plan mode is justified from the start.
Direct execution is never appropriate; plan mode should be the default for all tasks, however small or well-scoped.
Switching to plan mode mid-task automatically discards all prior work, so it must be avoided.

rationale.correct: The 'switch later' policy misreads the situation: a known large-scale architectural refactor has complexity that is stated up front, not merely potential. That is exactly the profile plan mode is designed for, so you should start in plan mode rather than wait for surprises.

distractors.A: This invents a false constraint; the flaw in 'switch later' is that it waits for stated complexity to resurface, not that switching is technically impossible.
distractors.C: Overcorrecting to 'plan mode for everything' is wrong; direct execution is the right choice for simple, well-scoped changes.
distractors.D: This relies on a fabricated side effect; the real objection is about when to plan, not about work being auto-discarded on a mode switch.

scenario: For a large restructuring with unresolved design questions, a developer proposes skipping plan mode and instead writing one very detailed direct-execution prompt that specifies exactly how every module should be built.
stem: Why is this weaker than using plan mode?

options.text: Detailed prompts exceed the model's input limit, so a prompt specifying each module's build cannot be processed.
Direct execution ignores prompt instructions, so the detail would have no effect.
It presumes the structure is known, but the open design questions require exploring the code first.
Plan mode is faster in every case, so detailed direct-execution prompts are always the slower option.

rationale.correct: Comprehensive upfront instructions presuppose you already know the right structure. With unresolved design questions, that knowledge does not yet exist; plan mode's safe exploration is what surfaces the dependencies and options needed to make those decisions well.

distractors.A: The weakness is conceptual, not a token-limit failure; a long prompt can be processed but still cannot substitute for exploration.
distractors.B: Direct execution does follow prompt instructions; the problem is that the instructions encode assumptions that have not been validated against the code.
distractors.D: Plan mode is not universally faster—it adds overhead for simple work; the real issue is that this task's unknowns demand exploration before committing.

scenario: You ask Claude to "normalize the customer name field" in a data-cleaning script. Across runs, Claude interprets this inconsistently: sometimes it title-cases, sometimes it strips middle initials, sometimes it reorders "Last, First" into "First Last", and sometimes it leaves suffixes like "Jr." and sometimes removes them. Rewriting the prose description a fourth time has not converged the behavior.
stem: What is the most effective next step to communicate the transformation you actually want?

options.text: Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples (e.g., `"SMITH, john q"` → `"John Q. Smith"`) on representative cases.
Add the instruction "be careful and precise about name normalization" to the prompt to raise the model's attention to the field.
Lower the temperature to 0 so the model produces the same interpretation of the prose every time.
Switch to a larger model so it can infer the intended normalization rules from the existing prose description.

rationale.correct: When a prose description is interpreted inconsistently, concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate the expected transformation. Two or three representative examples pin down casing, ordering, suffix handling, and punctuation unambiguously in a way that repeated prose rewrites cannot.

distractors.B: Vague reinforcement like "be careful and precise" adds no new information about the transformation rules; the ambiguity is in what the rules are, not in how hard the model tries.
distractors.C: Temperature 0 makes output deterministic for a fixed prompt but does not resolve which of several valid interpretations is intended; it would just lock in one arbitrary reading of the ambiguous prose.
distractors.D: A larger model still has to guess the unstated rules; the prose is genuinely underspecified, so no model can reliably infer suffix or ordering conventions that were never stated. Examples supply the missing specification.

scenario: You need a `parse_duration` function that turns strings like "1h30m", "90m", and "2h" into total seconds, and you already know the tricky edge cases (missing units, zero values, whitespace, uppercase). You want to iterate toward a correct implementation with tight feedback.
stem: Which workflow best applies test-driven iteration for progressive improvement?

options.text: Ask Claude to implement `parse_duration` first, then write tests afterward to confirm whatever behavior it produced.
Ask Claude to implement the function and manually eyeball a few outputs, re-prompting with "that looks wrong, try again" when something seems off.
Write a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases, and performance first, then have Claude implement and iterate by sharing the specific failing tests each round.
Write the test suite but keep it private, sharing only a summary like "3 of 12 tests fail" so Claude reasons about likely causes without seeing the assertions.

rationale.correct: Test-driven iteration means writing a test suite that encodes expected behavior, edge cases, and performance requirements before implementation, then iterating by sharing the concrete test failures. Each failure gives Claude a precise, verifiable target, so improvement is progressive and measurable rather than guesswork.

distractors.A: Writing tests after implementation lets the tests conform to whatever the code happens to do, so they validate accidental behavior rather than driving it toward the intended specification.
distractors.B: Eyeballing outputs and re-prompting with "try again" gives no concrete target and does not systematically cover the edge cases you already identified; it is exactly the vague-feedback loop TDD replaces.
distractors.D: Sharing only a failure count withholds the specific assertions Claude needs to correct behavior; the value of sharing failures is the concrete input, expected, and actual values, not the tally.

scenario: You are about to have Claude design a caching layer for a service in a domain you know only superficially. You suspect there are important considerations (invalidation, stampede protection, staleness tolerance) you have not thought through, and you do not want Claude to silently pick defaults that bite you later.
stem: How should you apply the interview pattern before implementation?

options.text: Instruct Claude to implement its single best-guess design immediately, then list any assumptions it made in a comment block afterward.
Ask Claude to first interview you with clarifying questions on invalidation, staleness, failure modes, and concurrency before coding.
Provide input/output examples of cache hits and misses so Claude can infer the full design from the examples alone.
Give Claude the full requirements in one message and ask it to generate three complete implementations to compare.

rationale.correct: The interview pattern has Claude ask you questions before implementing, surfacing design considerations (invalidation, staleness tolerance, failure modes, concurrency) you may not have anticipated. This is especially valuable in unfamiliar domains, where the risk is unknown unknowns rather than an ambiguous but well-understood transformation.

distractors.A: Implementing a best guess and documenting assumptions afterward still bakes in unexamined defaults; the point of the interview is to expose those decisions before code exists, when they are cheap to change.
distractors.C: Input/output examples clarify a known transformation but cannot surface hidden architectural considerations like invalidation or stampede protection; you do not yet know enough to write the right examples.
distractors.D: Generating three implementations multiplies unexamined assumptions rather than surfacing them; you would still lack the criteria to judge which design's hidden trade-offs are acceptable.

scenario: Reviewing a generated pagination module, you find three problems: (1) the page-size default is 20 but the API contract says 25, (2) the offset calculation assumes 1-based page numbers while the caller passes 0-based, and (3) the total-count query and the item query use different WHERE clauses, so the last page can be miscomputed. Fixing the offset math changes which items land on the last page, which changes how the count mismatch manifests, and the page-size default feeds directly into both the offset and the count logic.
stem: How should you deliver this feedback to Claude?

options.text: Report all three issues in a single detailed message, since the fixes interact and a coherent solution must reconcile them together.
Report only issue 1 first, and reveal issues 2 and 3 in separate follow-up messages after each prior fix is confirmed.
Report the issues in three separate parallel sessions so each fix is developed independently, then merge the three patches.
Report only the highest-severity issue (the count mismatch) and let Claude discover the other two on its own during the fix.

rationale.correct: When issues interact—here the page-size default, offset base, and count/item query alignment all influence the same last-page computation—providing them together in a single detailed message lets Claude reason about the fixes holistically and produce a coherent solution rather than a series of patches that undo one another.

distractors.B: Sequential fixing is appropriate for independent problems; for interacting ones it causes churn, because each fix is made without visibility into the constraints the other issues impose and may have to be redone.
distractors.C: Developing interacting fixes in isolated parallel sessions guarantees conflicting assumptions (e.g., page base, size) that will collide at merge time; isolation is the opposite of what interacting issues need.
distractors.D: Withholding two known, interacting issues forces Claude to fix the count mismatch against incorrect offset and page-size assumptions, so the fix is likely wrong until the other two surface anyway.

scenario: In a utility module, you notice three unrelated defects: a typo in a log message, a docstring that describes the wrong return type, and a missing `None` guard in a separate helper. None of the three touches the same code path or shares any state, and each fix is self-contained.
stem: What is the best refinement strategy?

options.text: Bundle all three into one large message because sending more context per turn is always more efficient.
Fix them sequentially or as clearly separated items, since they don't interact and each can be verified alone.
Rewrite the entire module from scratch so all three defects disappear at once regardless of their independence.
Ignore the typo and docstring as low value and fix only the `None` guard, since independent issues rarely matter.

rationale.correct: Independent problems that share no code path or state can be fixed sequentially (or as cleanly separated items) because no fix constrains another. This keeps each change small, individually verifiable, and easy to review—the mirror image of the single-message approach reserved for interacting issues.

distractors.A: "More context is always better" is a misconception; bundling is chosen because issues interact, not for raw efficiency. Independent issues gain nothing from being forced together and can obscure per-fix verification.
distractors.C: A full rewrite is disproportionate to three tiny independent defects and risks introducing new regressions across code that was otherwise correct.
distractors.D: Independence is not a reason to skip fixes; correctness and clarity issues still warrant fixing. The question is how to sequence them, not whether to drop them.

scenario: A data-migration script Claude wrote works on typical rows but mishandles edge cases: rows where `middle_name` is `NULL` get the literal string "None" written into the target column, and rows where `amount` is `NULL` are silently dropped instead of migrated with a null. Your prose instruction "handle nulls correctly" has not fixed it.
stem: What is the most reliable way to correct the edge-case handling?

options.text: Provide specific test cases: example input rows containing NULLs paired with the exact expected output rows.
Repeat the instruction "handle nulls correctly" more emphatically and add "do not make mistakes with null values".
Ask Claude to add a broad `try/except` around the migration so any null-related error is swallowed at runtime.
Instruct Claude to skip any row containing a NULL so the edge cases never reach the transformation logic.

rationale.correct: Edge-case handling is best fixed with specific test cases pairing example input (rows with NULLs) and the exact expected output, so the desired null handling is concrete and verifiable. This turns the vague "handle nulls correctly" into checkable targets—e.g., NULL `middle_name` maps to a null column value, not the string "None"; NULL `amount` migrates as null rather than being dropped.

distractors.B: Emphatic restatement adds no information about what "correct" null handling means; the model already tried and produced two different wrong behaviors, so it needs concrete expected outputs, not more emphasis.
distractors.C: Swallowing errors with a broad `try/except` hides the defect rather than fixing it and can silently drop or corrupt more rows, making the migration untrustworthy.
distractors.D: Skipping rows with NULLs discards valid data; the requirement is to migrate nulls faithfully, so dropping them is a data-loss bug, not a fix.

scenario: A teammate proposes: "For any refinement task, the fastest path is always to give Claude every requirement up front in one big message and let it produce the final implementation." You are coaching them on when each iterative-refinement technique actually applies.
stem: Which correction best captures how to choose among the techniques?

options.text: Always front-load everything in one message; the interview pattern and test-driven iteration are only useful when the requirements are trivial to state.
Match technique to situation: I/O examples for inconsistent prose, tests for verifiable behavior, interviews for unfamiliar domains, one message only for interacting issues.
Never provide requirements up front; the interview pattern should replace all other techniques because asking questions first is universally optimal for surfacing intent.
Prefer sequential single-issue messages in every case, because smaller messages are easier for the model to process and verify than one combined message.

rationale.correct: The techniques are situational, not ranked. Concrete input/output examples fix inconsistently interpreted prose; test-driven iteration drives verifiable behavior via shared failures; the interview pattern surfaces unanticipated considerations in unfamiliar domains; and a single detailed message is for interacting issues while independent issues are best handled sequentially. Choosing correctly depends on the problem, not a one-size-fits-all rule.

distractors.A: Front-loading everything is right only for interacting issues; the interview pattern and TDD add the most value precisely on non-trivial, ambiguous, or unfamiliar work, not on trivial tasks.
distractors.C: The interview pattern is targeted at surfacing unknowns in unfamiliar domains; using it universally wastes turns when requirements are already clear and better expressed as examples or tests.
distractors.D: Sequential single-issue messages fit independent problems; forcing interacting issues into separate turns causes rework, and "smaller is always easier" ignores that interacting fixes need shared context.

scenario: You wrote a failing test suite for a `csv_to_records` parser first. On the current iteration, 4 of 18 tests fail, all on quoted fields that contain embedded commas and escaped quotes. You want to guide Claude to a fix in the next turn.
stem: What should you share to make the iteration most productive?

options.text: Tell Claude "some tests are still failing, please make them pass" without further detail so it explores broadly.
Delete the 4 failing tests so the suite is green and move on, since the passing majority indicates the parser mostly works.
Paste the 4 failing test cases with their exact inputs, expected outputs, and the actual outputs the parser produced.
Ask Claude to rewrite the parser from scratch using a different algorithm, discarding the current implementation and its partial progress.

rationale.correct: Test-driven iteration works by sharing the concrete failures: the exact inputs, expected outputs, and actual outputs of the 4 failing cases. This localizes the defect to quoted-field parsing and gives Claude a precise, verifiable target for the next revision, so it can fix the quoted-field handling specifically — which is how progressive improvement compounds.

distractors.A: "Some tests are failing, make them pass" withholds the diagnostic detail that makes shared failures useful; broad exploration without the specific assertions is slow and may regress currently passing cases.
distractors.B: Deleting failing tests hides a real defect in quoted-field handling and defeats the purpose of writing the suite first; the tests encode required behavior, not optional nice-to-haves.
distractors.D: A from-scratch rewrite throws away 14 passing behaviors and the progress made; the failures are narrowly scoped to quoted fields and call for a targeted fix, not wholesale replacement.

scenario: Your CI pipeline runs `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"` as a build step, but the job hangs indefinitely. The logs show Claude Code is waiting for interactive input that never arrives in the headless runner.
stem: What is the correct way to run Claude Code so it processes the prompt and exits without waiting for interactive input?

options.text: Add the `-p` (or `--print`) flag: `claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`.
Set an environment variable before the command: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`.
Add a `--batch` flag: `claude --batch "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`.
Redirect stdin from `/dev/null`: `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" < /dev/null`.

rationale.correct: The `-p` / `--print` flag is the documented way to run Claude Code non-interactively: it processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits without opening an interactive session, which is exactly what a CI/CD runner needs.

distractors.B: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` is not a real Claude Code environment variable; inventing an env toggle does not change the CLI's interactive default.
distractors.C: There is no `--batch` flag in Claude Code; this confuses the CLI with the separate Message Batches API and does not disable interactive mode.
distractors.D: Redirecting stdin from `/dev/null` is a Unix workaround that may cause the session to error rather than cleanly print-and-exit; the supported mechanism is the `-p` flag, not a shell redirect.

scenario: A GitHub Actions workflow invokes `claude -p` to review each PR, and a downstream step parses the result to post individual findings as inline comments on the exact files and lines. Right now Claude returns prose, and the parser breaks whenever the wording varies.
stem: Which change most reliably produces machine-parseable findings the workflow can turn into inline PR comments?

options.text: Increase the runner timeout so Claude has more time to format the response consistently before the job is cut off.
Keep the prose output but append "respond only in valid JSON" to the prompt and parse whatever text comes back.
Run with `--output-format json` plus `--json-schema` defining each finding's file, line, severity, and message.
Post the entire prose response as a single top-level PR comment instead of parsing individual findings.

rationale.correct: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` forces Claude Code to return structured output conforming to a schema you define, giving the workflow stable fields (file path, line number, severity, message) it can map directly onto inline PR comments.

distractors.A: A longer timeout addresses hangs or slow runs, not output structure; the parser fails on format, not duration.
distractors.B: A prompt instruction only makes valid JSON probable; the model can still emit malformed or extra prose, which is precisely the fragility the schema flags eliminate.
distractors.D: Dumping prose into one comment abandons the requirement for per-file, per-line inline comments and does not make the output parseable.

scenario: The same Claude Code session that just generated a new caching layer is asked, within that same session, to review its own diff before opening the PR. Reviewers notice the self-review consistently rates the code highly and misses defects that a teammate later catches.
stem: What is the most effective structural fix for the weak review quality?

options.text: Keep the review in the generating session but lower the temperature so the model applies more critical, consistent scrutiny.
Run the review in an independent Claude Code instance that did not generate the code, invoked fresh via `claude -p` in CI.
Keep the review in the generating session and add "be extremely strict and skeptical" to the review prompt.
Keep the review in the generating session but switch to a larger-context model so it can hold the whole diff.

rationale.correct: Session context isolation is the point: the session that produced the code carries the assumptions and justifications that led to it, so it is biased toward approving its own work. An independent instance reviews the diff without that baggage and catches issues the author-session rationalizes away.

distractors.A: Temperature changes sampling randomness, not the self-justification bias baked into the generating session's context.
distractors.C: A sterner prompt is a probabilistic nudge that cannot overcome the structural conflict of interest of reviewing within the session that made the decisions.
distractors.D: The problem is contaminated context, not context capacity; a bigger window still carries the same self-serving assumptions.

scenario: Your automated reviewer runs on every push to a PR. After a developer pushes a follow-up commit, the reviewer re-runs on the full diff and re-posts the same three findings it already commented on last time, plus one genuinely new issue. Developers are frustrated by the duplicate noise.
stem: How should you change the re-run so it comments only on new or still-unaddressed issues?

options.text: Disable the reviewer on all commits after the first, so each PR gets a single review pass and earlier findings are not re-posted.
Deduplicate in the posting script by string-matching each new comment's text against existing PR comments and dropping exact repeats.
Lower the review's sensitivity so it surfaces fewer findings overall, which reduces how many repeats can appear on each run.
Include the prior review's findings in context and instruct Claude to report only issues that are new or still unaddressed.

rationale.correct: Passing the previous findings into context and telling Claude to report only new or unresolved issues lets the model reason about what has already been raised and whether later commits addressed it, so re-runs add signal instead of repeating comments.

distractors.A: Running only once defeats the purpose of continuous review; later commits can introduce new defects that go unreviewed.
distractors.B: Exact string matching is brittle: reworded or line-shifted findings slip through as duplicates, and it cannot tell whether an issue was actually fixed.
distractors.C: Reducing sensitivity suppresses real findings across the board rather than solving the specific duplicate-comment problem.

scenario: A CI-invoked Claude Code review keeps flagging the team's intentional patterns (custom logger, repository abstraction) as problems and misses the security checks the team actually cares about. Nothing about the team's standards or review priorities is available to the CI instance.
stem: What is the best way to give the CI-invoked Claude Code the project context it needs to review consistently with the team's expectations?

options.text: Commit a CLAUDE.md documenting testing standards, review criteria, and accepted project patterns.
Paste the standards into each developer's local Claude Code settings so every session they start applies them.
Fine-tune a custom model on the repository so the team's standards are baked into the weights the review uses.
Add the standards as a comment block inside the CI YAML file that launches the job, next to the `claude` invocation.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for supplying project context (testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria, accepted patterns) to Claude Code; committed to the repo, the CI-invoked instance reads it as project context automatically and reviews against the team's actual expectations.

distractors.B: Local per-developer settings do not travel into the CI runner's checkout, so the automated review never sees them.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning is disproportionate and slow for encoding evolving team conventions that a committed CLAUDE.md handles directly.
distractors.D: A comment in the workflow YAML is not read as project context by Claude Code; it does not influence the review the way CLAUDE.md does.

scenario: A CI job uses Claude Code to generate additional tests for changed modules. The generated tests largely duplicate scenarios already covered in the existing suite, so reviewers spend time deleting near-identical cases.
stem: What change most directly reduces the duplicate test suggestions?

options.text: Ask Claude to generate twice as many tests so more of them happen to be novel, then keep the new ones.
Run the generation at a higher temperature so the outputs vary more and repeat existing scenarios less often.
Generate the tests without any existing context and rely on reviewers to prune the duplicates afterward.
Provide the existing test files in context so Claude can see current coverage and target untested scenarios.

rationale.correct: Including the existing test files lets Claude see what is already covered, so it targets genuine gaps instead of re-proposing scenarios the suite already exercises, directly cutting duplicate output.

distractors.A: Producing more tests scales up duplicates rather than eliminating them; volume is not the problem.
distractors.B: Higher temperature adds superficial variation but does not give the model knowledge of existing coverage, so overlaps persist.
distractors.C: Pushing pruning onto reviewers is the current painful workflow; it does not reduce the duplicate generation at the source.

scenario: A teammate argues the CI review is unreliable and proposes several changes. You need to separate the fixes that actually address CI integration from the ones based on misconceptions.
stem: Which statement about integrating Claude Code into CI/CD is correct?

options.text: A larger context window is what lets Claude Code run inside a headless CI runner without hanging on long diffs.
The `-p` flag runs Claude Code non-interactively, and `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` yields structured findings.
The generating session is the ideal reviewer of its own diff because it already holds all the relevant context.
Re-running the review on each commit inherently avoids duplicate comments without needing prior findings in context or extra flags.

rationale.correct: Non-interactive execution comes from the `-p`/`--print` flag, and machine-parseable output comes from `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema`; together they let a pipeline run Claude Code unattended and post structured findings.

distractors.A: Context window size has nothing to do with interactivity; the hang is fixed by `-p`, not by a bigger window.
distractors.C: Session context isolation is why the generating session is a poor self-reviewer; its own assumptions bias it toward approval, so an independent instance is preferred.
distractors.D: Without the prior findings in context, a per-commit re-run re-reports the same issues; deduplication requires giving Claude the earlier findings and instructing it to report only new or unaddressed ones.

scenario: You are hardening a Claude Code CI review step that must (1) never block on input, (2) emit findings a script can post as inline comments, and (3) avoid re-posting issues raised on earlier commits of the same PR.
stem: Which combination of measures satisfies all three requirements?

options.text: Set `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` to suppress prompts; parse the prose output with a regex; and rely on the posting script to string-match away duplicates.
Use the `--batch` flag for unattended runs; ask the prompt to "return JSON"; and re-run on the full diff each commit without prior findings.
Invoke with `-p`; use `--output-format json` plus `--json-schema`; and pass prior findings in context, reporting only new or unaddressed issues.
Redirect stdin from `/dev/null` so nothing can prompt; post the raw prose as one comment; and lower sensitivity so fewer duplicates appear.

rationale.correct: Each requirement maps to a specific, documented mechanism: `-p` for non-interactive execution, `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` for parseable structured findings, and passing prior findings into context with report-only-new instructions for deduplication.

distractors.A: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` is not a real variable, regex over prose is fragile, and string-matching cannot tell whether an issue was fixed—so none of the three requirements are met reliably.
distractors.B: `--batch` does not exist in Claude Code, a prompt request for JSON is not schema-enforced, and re-running without prior findings guarantees duplicate comments.
distractors.D: A stdin redirect is an unreliable workaround, single prose comments are not inline-postable, and lowering sensitivity suppresses real findings rather than deduplicating them.

scenario: Your code-review agent flags too many non-issues on the comment-accuracy check, and developers are starting to ignore its output.
stem: Which instruction is most likely to actually improve precision on the comment-accuracy category?

options.text: "Be conservative and only report comment issues you are highly confident are real problems."
"Flag a comment only when the behavior it claims contradicts what the code actually does."
"Check that all comments are accurate and up to date with the code they describe."
"Report the comment issues you consider most important for maintainers of this codebase."

rationale.correct: This is an explicit categorical criterion: it names the exact condition that qualifies a finding (claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior), so the model applies a consistent, checkable test rather than its own fuzzy notion of "accurate." Explicit criteria are what move precision, per the exam guide's contrast of the contradiction rule against "check that comments are accurate."

distractors.A: "Be conservative" and confidence gating do not define what counts as an issue; the model still uses its own vague standard for what to flag, so the false-positive mix is largely unchanged. General calibration instructions fail to improve precision.
distractors.C: "Accurate and up to date" is exactly the vague instruction the guide warns against; it invites flagging stylistic staleness and subjective mismatches, which drives false positives.
distractors.D: "Most important" is a subjective, non-categorical instruction that gives the model no checkable boundary, so it will not reliably reduce false positives.

scenario: A teammate proposes fixing your review agent's noisy output by prepending "Only report high-confidence findings and err on the side of caution" to every prompt.
stem: Why is this change unlikely to meaningfully reduce the false-positive rate?

options.text: Confidence instructions don't define which categories of issue qualify, so the model keeps applying its own vague threshold.
The model cannot process meta-instructions about its own confidence level, so it will effectively ignore the sentence entirely.
High-confidence filtering always suppresses true positives faster than false positives, so precision necessarily drops.
Confidence instructions only take effect when placed after the code under review, not before it in the prompt.

rationale.correct: General instructions like "be conservative" or "only high-confidence" do not tell the model what qualifies as a reportable issue. Without an explicit categorical boundary the model keeps using its own subjective standard, so the false-positive mix is essentially unchanged. The fix is specific criteria (which issues to report vs skip), not a confidence dial.

distractors.B: The model does process such phrasing; the problem is not that it is ignored but that it provides no concrete decision boundary.
distractors.C: This overstates a mechanism. The core failure is the absence of categorical criteria, not a guaranteed law that true positives are suppressed first.
distractors.D: Prompt position is not the issue; a vague confidence instruction fails regardless of where it appears.

scenario: Your security-review category is precise and trusted, but the "style" and "naming" categories fire constantly on acceptable local patterns. Developers now skim past every finding, including the security ones.
stem: What is the best immediate action to restore developer trust while you improve the noisy categories?

options.text: Lower the overall severity threshold so fewer findings of every type appear, including security, until the noise drops.
Add a global "be more conservative" instruction shared across all categories so each one reports less aggressively.
Temporarily disable the noisy style and naming categories, keeping the trusted categories active while you rewrite their criteria.
Leave everything on but add a disclaimer to each review telling developers to ignore style and naming findings until they improve.

rationale.correct: The guide's recommended move is to temporarily disable high-false-positive categories to restore trust while you improve their prompts. This stops the noise that is contaminating perception of the accurate categories, without weakening the categories that already work.

distractors.A: Suppressing findings across the board damages the trusted security category too, trading a precision problem for a recall problem where it hurts most.
distractors.B: A global "be conservative" instruction is the general-instruction anti-pattern; it does not define criteria and will not fix the noisy categories.
distractors.D: A disclaimer does not remove the noise; developers still have to triage it, and the erosion of trust in accurate categories continues.

scenario: Leadership asks why the accurate security category is being ignored even though its findings are almost always correct.
stem: Which explanation best captures the cross-category trust dynamic the exam emphasizes?

options.text: Security findings are inherently harder to act on, so developers defer them regardless of other categories.
A few high-false-positive categories erode confidence in the whole tool, so developers distrust even the accurate ones.
Precision in one category has no effect on how developers perceive the others; each category is judged on its own record.
Developers trust the categories that produce the largest number of findings, since volume signals thorough coverage.

rationale.correct: The guide states that high false-positive categories undermine confidence in the accurate categories. Trust is holistic: once developers learn the tool cries wolf in some categories, they discount all of its output, including the reliable security findings.

distractors.A: The problem is not intrinsic difficulty of security findings; it is contamination of trust from noisy categories.
distractors.C: This is the opposite of the guide's point; false positives in one category do spill over into perception of others.
distractors.D: Volume does not build trust; noisy high-volume categories are precisely what destroys it.

scenario: You are defining severity levels for your review agent so that classification is consistent across runs and reviewers.
stem: What is the most reliable way to get consistent severity classification?

options.text: Define each severity level with explicit criteria and a concrete code example of that level.
Instruct the model to "use its best judgment" to rank each finding's severity on a 1-to-5 scale.
Ask the model to assign severity based on how confident it feels that each finding is real.
Tell the model to mark anything security-related as high and everything else as low, as a simple rule.

rationale.correct: The guide's skill is defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each level. Anchoring each severity to a described condition plus a worked example gives the model a checkable rubric, producing consistent classification across findings and runs.

distractors.B: "Best judgment" on a bare numeric scale is the vague-instruction pattern; without criteria per level, classification drifts run to run.
distractors.C: Confidence is not severity; a low-impact issue can be high-confidence. Conflating them produces inconsistent, miscalibrated levels.
distractors.D: A blanket security=high mapping ignores actual impact (e.g., a theoretical issue in dead code) and misclassifies non-security bugs that are genuinely severe.

scenario: You must write criteria that tell the review agent which issues to report and which to skip.
stem: Which pairing best reflects precision-oriented criteria design per the guide?

options.text: Report: findings the model is confident about. Skip: findings it is unsure about or would otherwise hedge on.
Report: everything, then let developers filter in the PR UI. Skip: nothing.
Report: genuine bugs and security vulnerabilities. Skip: minor style preferences and established local patterns.
Report: whatever appears most frequently in the diff. Skip: rare, one-off patterns that are more likely to be noise.

rationale.correct: The guide's skill is writing specific review criteria that define which issues to report (bugs, security) versus skip (minor style, local patterns), rather than relying on confidence-based filtering. This categorical report/skip boundary is what raises precision.

distractors.A: This is confidence-based filtering, which the guide explicitly says does not improve precision; it defines no categories.
distractors.B: Reporting everything maximizes false positives and pushes triage cost onto developers, destroying trust.
distractors.D: Frequency is unrelated to whether something is a genuine issue; rare patterns can be the most serious bugs.

scenario: Two reviewers running the same agent on the same file disagree on whether a finding is "medium" or "high" severity, and the model's own labels vary between runs.
stem: What change most directly addresses this inconsistency?

options.text: Increase the temperature so the model considers more options before settling on a final severity label.
Replace abstract severity labels with per-level criteria plus a concrete code example for each level.
Add "be consistent with severity labels across runs" to the system prompt.
Ask the model to make several independent severity guesses and report the average as its final label.

rationale.correct: Inconsistency comes from an undefined boundary between levels. Giving each severity explicit criteria and a concrete code example makes the boundary between medium and high explicit and checkable, so both reviewers and repeated runs land on the same classification.

distractors.A: Raising temperature increases variability, making labels less consistent, not more.
distractors.C: "Be consistent" is a vague meta-instruction with no criteria; it does not define the level boundaries that are actually ambiguous.
distractors.D: Averaging noisy self-estimates without defined criteria still centers on an undefined boundary; the disagreement about what medium vs high means persists.

scenario: After adding explicit categorical criteria to the bug and security categories, precision jumps. A stakeholder now wants to re-enable the previously disabled style category.
stem: What is the correct precondition before re-enabling the style category?

options.text: Re-enable it immediately with a "be conservative" instruction, since the other categories are now accurate and trusted by developers.
Rewrite the style category with explicit criteria for what qualifies and what to skip, then verify its false-positive rate is low.
Re-enable it but lower every category's severity so the extra style findings look less alarming to developers.
Re-enable it and rely on developers to mute the category themselves if it becomes noisy again.

rationale.correct: Disabling was a temporary trust-restoration measure; the guide pairs it with improving the prompts for those categories. Re-enable only after the style category has explicit categorical criteria (which style issues qualify, which acceptable local patterns to skip) and a verified low false-positive rate, or it will re-contaminate trust in the accurate categories.

distractors.A: A "be conservative" instruction is the general-instruction anti-pattern that did not fix the category before and will not now; the noise returns.
distractors.C: Lowering all severities damages the trusted categories and does nothing to make the style criteria precise.
distractors.D: Shifting triage to developers is exactly the dynamic that eroded trust; re-enabling an unimproved noisy category repeats the original mistake.

scenario: Your code-review agent must emit findings in a fixed format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix). You have already written a long, detailed instruction block describing the format, yet the agent's output remains inconsistent across runs: severity is sometimes omitted, and the fix is occasionally merged into the issue field.
stem: Detailed instructions alone are producing inconsistent output. What is the most effective next step to achieve consistently formatted, actionable findings?

options.text: Add 2-4 few-shot examples, each showing a complete finding in the exact target format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix).
Rewrite the instruction block to be even more explicit and exhaustive, enumerating every formatting rule as a longer numbered list.
Lower the temperature to 0 so the model produces the same formatting deterministically on every run.
Split the task into four separate prompts, one per field, and concatenate the results into a single finding afterward.

rationale.correct: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results. Showing 2-4 complete findings in the exact target format demonstrates the structure directly, which the model imitates more reliably than it follows prose rules.

distractors.B: Escalating instruction detail is precisely the approach that already failed; more prose rules do not fix inconsistency the way a concrete format demonstration does.
distractors.C: Temperature 0 increases determinism but does not teach the model what the correct format is; a deterministic run can still consistently omit severity if the format was never demonstrated.
distractors.D: Decomposing into per-field prompts adds orchestration complexity and stitching logic while ignoring the direct fix: demonstrating the whole format once with examples.

scenario: A teammate proposes adding few-shot examples to a prompt that must handle a handful of ambiguous edge cases (e.g., which tool to select for an underspecified request). They suggest pasting 30 examples harvested from past logs to be safe.
stem: What is the recommended guidance on how many few-shot examples to include for these ambiguous cases?
