Keep the current reasoning budget and stream the responses, since streaming reduces total generation time.

rationale.correct: Reasoning improves accuracy on hard tasks but costs latency and tokens, so match it to difficulty. Routing keeps quality where it matters and speeds the majority of simple queries.

distractors.A: Removing reasoning everywhere would hurt the policy questions that benefit from it, trading one problem for another.
distractors.B: A higher output cap affects truncation, not speed, and would not make simple lookups faster.
distractors.D: Streaming improves perceived latency but does not reduce total generation time, and the reasoning itself still delays the first visible token.

scenario: A RAG assistant retrieves 40 chunks per query. An evaluation shows answer quality plateaus after about 8 chunks, while latency and token cost keep rising and the answers sometimes cite irrelevant chunks.
stem: What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Increase retrieval to 100 chunks so that the model has more evidence from which to select the most relevant material.
Keep 40 chunks but ask the model in the prompt to ignore chunks that do not seem relevant to the question.
Keep 40 chunks and switch to a larger model, which can handle long contexts without losing track of relevant text.
Reduce retrieval to roughly the top 8 to 10 chunks, optionally after reranking a larger pool, and confirm on the evaluation set.

rationale.correct: Beyond the knee of the quality curve, extra chunks add cost, latency, and distraction. Trimming the depth, with reranking to put the best chunks first, restores efficiency while the evaluation guards quality.

distractors.A: More chunks moves further past the plateau, increasing cost and distraction with no accuracy benefit.
distractors.B: Telling the model to ignore chunks still pays for their tokens and latency, and distraction can still affect the answer.
distractors.C: A larger model is slower and costlier and does not remove the unnecessary retrieval work.

scenario: A report generator produces 1,500-word answers that take about 40 seconds. The web UI shows a spinner until the whole response arrives, and users abandon the page, although the full answer is what they need.
stem: Which change best improves the experience?

options.text: Switch to the batch API, which processes requests more cheaply and so should reduce waiting for users.
Poll the API once a second for the finished response so that the UI can display it the moment it is ready.
Cap the output at 300 words so that generation finishes within about 8 seconds for each request.
Stream the response so text appears as it is generated, which cuts time to first visible output.

rationale.correct: Streaming does not shorten total generation time, but it removes the blank wait by showing progress immediately, which is what drives abandonment in interactive long-form answers.

distractors.A: Batch processing is for non-urgent work with no latency guarantee, so it would make interactive waiting worse.
distractors.B: Polling still shows nothing until the full response exists, so the user sees the same blank wait.
distractors.C: Truncating to 300 words fails the requirement for full 1,500-word reports.

scenario: A law firm deploys a Claude assistant that summarizes deposition transcripts for attorneys. The team must pick an automated quality metric before the pilot. Summaries are free-form, and attorneys care that every stated fact is traceable to the transcript.
stem: Which metric best measures what the attorneys actually care about?

options.text: Word-overlap score (ROUGE) against one attorney-written reference summary per transcript.
The average number of words per summary, tracked to keep summaries consistently concise.
Share of factual claims in a summary that the source transcript supports, judged by rubric.
The percentage of attorneys who click the thumbs-up button after reading a summary.

rationale.correct: Claim-level support against the source directly measures faithfulness, the stated success criterion, and can be scored by a rubric-driven grader and human spot checks. It is task-specific and measurable.

distractors.A: Overlap with a single reference penalizes valid paraphrases and rewards copying; it does not detect an unsupported claim that happens to share words.
distractors.B: Length is a style property; a short summary can be entirely wrong, so it says nothing about faithfulness.
distractors.D: Thumbs-up is a useful satisfaction signal but is sparse and biased, and attorneys rarely re-verify facts when they vote.

scenario: An insurer uses Claude to triage incoming claims into 'fast-track', 'standard', and 'investigate-for-fraud'. Missing a fraudulent claim costs far more than sending a legitimate one to the investigation queue, though the investigation team has limited capacity.
stem: Which metric design best reflects the business risk?

options.text: Overall accuracy across the three queues, since it summarizes performance in one number.
Mean latency per triage decision, since faster triage reduces the claim backlog.
Total tokens consumed per claim, since cost per decision determines the program's ROI.
Recall on the fraud class with a floor on precision, so the investigation queue stays workable.

rationale.correct: The costs are asymmetric: the metric must emphasize catching fraud (recall on that class) while a precision floor protects the limited investigation capacity. Per-class metrics expose the trade-off that accuracy hides.

distractors.A: Fraud is rare, so overall accuracy can stay high while most fraud is missed; it ignores the asymmetric cost of errors.
distractors.B: Latency matters operationally but says nothing about whether the right claims reach the right queue.
distractors.C: Token cost is a legitimate secondary metric, but optimizing it does not measure triage correctness, the primary risk.

scenario: A healthcare provider adds a Claude voice-style scheduling assistant. Callers abandon the interaction when pauses are noticeable. The current dashboard shows a mean response time of 1.4 seconds, and the product owner says that is acceptable.
stem: What is the best change to how latency is defined for this use case?

options.text: Track the 95th and 99th percentile time to first token, since tail pauses drive abandonment for an interactive channel.
Keep the mean, but average over a longer window so that short bursts of slowness are smoothed out.
Track total tokens generated per call, since fewer tokens means a faster-feeling conversation.
Measure just server-side processing time and exclude network and queueing delay, which the team cannot control.

rationale.correct: For interactive channels users experience the tail, not the mean, and time to first token captures when the response begins. Percentiles expose the slow minority that a mean of 1.4 seconds hides.

distractors.B: Longer averaging windows hide exactly the short, bad episodes that cause abandonment.
distractors.C: Output volume affects total time, but it is a cause, not the user-perceived metric; it does not measure the pause callers notice.
distractors.D: Users experience end-to-end delay including queueing and network, so excluding them understates the problem.

scenario: A bank's Claude-powered assistant can read customer emails and call internal tools. Security asks the AI team for a metric that shows whether the assistant resists prompt injection embedded in those emails, and wants a number it can track release over release.
stem: Which metric best serves that goal?

options.text: Count of requests the input filter blocked in production last month, reported on a monthly dashboard.
Fraction of curated injection attempts, run against each release, that cause an unauthorized action.
A penetration test performed once a year by an external firm, summarized in a written report.
The overall refusal rate of the assistant on all production traffic, shown as a rolling average.

rationale.correct: Attack success rate on a maintained adversarial set, executed for every release, is repeatable, comparable over time, and measures the outcome that matters (unauthorized action) rather than activity.

distractors.A: Blocked-request counts measure filter activity, not whether attacks that get through succeed, and they depend on the traffic mix.
distractors.C: An annual test is valuable but too infrequent to detect regressions introduced by each prompt or model change.
distractors.D: Refusal rate conflates blocked attacks with legitimate refusals and says nothing about injections that succeeded.

scenario: A legal-tech company is building a Claude-based classifier that tags incoming contracts by type and risk. They have six months of historical contracts and three paralegals available for labeling, and they need an evaluation dataset before tuning prompts.
stem: Which approach to building the dataset is best?

options.text: Sample real contracts to match production type frequencies, add rare types and known tricky cases, and have experts label them.
Have Claude generate several thousand synthetic contracts and label them with Claude, so the set scales without human effort.
Use just the contracts that earlier versions of the prompt already classified correctly, so the baseline starts high.
Write fifty clean, typical contracts by hand so each example is unambiguous and the scores are stable.

rationale.correct: A useful golden set mirrors production inputs and deliberately over-represents rare and difficult cases, with trusted human labels. That makes scores predictive and lets the team see where the system is weak.

distractors.B: Synthetic data labeled by the same model measures agreement with itself, not correctness, and inherits its blind spots.
distractors.C: Filtering to already-correct cases removes exactly the failures the dataset exists to reveal.
distractors.D: Clean hand-written examples are easier than production and miss ambiguity, so scores overstate quality.

scenario: A retailer's support assistant must (a) quote the refund amount from a policy table and (b) respond with an empathetic tone. The team wants automated evaluation for both checks in CI and needs each to be trustworthy.
stem: Which grading assignment is most appropriate?

options.text: Use an LLM judge for both, since a judge handles any criterion and keeps the pipeline uniform.
Use exact string match for both, since automated checks must be deterministic to be trusted.
Check refund amounts in code; grade tone with a rubric-based LLM judge validated against humans.
Use human reviewers for both on every CI run, since only people can judge correctness and tone.

rationale.correct: Objective, checkable properties belong in deterministic code, which is cheap and exact. Subjective qualities need a judge, which must be calibrated against human ratings to be trusted.

distractors.A: Using a judge for a numeric lookup adds cost and noise where an exact comparison is available.
distractors.B: Tone cannot be verified by string match, so the check would be meaningless or brittle.
distractors.D: Human review on every CI run is slow and costly; humans are better used to calibrate the judge and review samples.

scenario: A healthcare administrator's team adopts an LLM judge to score whether patient-facing answers follow the clinic's scheduling policy. The judge's scores look plausible, and the team wants to use it as the release gate next week.
stem: What should the team do before using the judge as a gate?

options.text: Raise the judge's temperature so that scores average out across repeated runs and reduce any systematic error.
Compare the judge's verdicts with expert human labels on a sample, and fix the rubric where they diverge.
Ask the judge to explain its score in more detail, since longer explanations indicate it is more reliable.
Use the same model that wrote the answers as the judge, since it knows the intent behind each response.

rationale.correct: A judge is itself a model and must be validated: measure agreement against human labels on a representative sample and refine the rubric where it disagrees. Only then is its score a trustworthy gate.

distractors.A: Randomness does not remove a systematic bias in the rubric or the judge; it adds noise.
distractors.C: Verbose explanations can be persuasive but wrong; they are not evidence that verdicts match human judgment.
distractors.D: A judge sharing the generator's blind spots tends to favor its own style and errors, which weakens independence.

scenario: An education company tunes a grading-feedback prompt by adding examples drawn from its 200-item evaluation set into the prompt. The evaluation score climbs from 71% to 93%, but teachers report little real-world improvement.
stem: What is the most likely problem and the right fix?

options.text: The model has become overconfident; lower the temperature so that the evaluation set is scored more conservatively.
The evaluation set is too large; reduce it to the few items where the prompt is expected to improve.
The eval items leaked into the prompt, inflating scores; keep a separate held-out set that is never used for prompt tuning.
Teachers are mistaken; the 93% score is the authoritative measure and no further validation is needed.

rationale.correct: Putting evaluation items in the prompt contaminates the test, so the score measures memorization rather than generalization. A held-out set that is never used for tuning gives an honest estimate.

distractors.A: Temperature does not address contamination; the score is inflated because the answers are effectively in the prompt.
distractors.B: Shrinking the set toward expected wins makes the metric less representative, which worsens the problem.
distractors.D: Ignoring contradicting field feedback treats a contaminated number as truth; real-world signal is a warning here.

scenario: A retailer wants to know whether a rewritten product-advice prompt increases the share of chats that end in a purchase. The engineer proposes deploying it to everyone on Monday and comparing this week's conversion with last week's.
stem: What is the better way to measure the effect?

options.text: Compare this week with last week, but adjust for the number of working days so the periods are comparable.
Randomly assign concurrent traffic between the old and new prompts and compare conversion across the two groups.
Ask the sales team whether chats seem better, since they review a sample of conversations each day.
Deploy the new prompt to just the busiest hours, which gives more data for the comparison.

rationale.correct: Concurrent random assignment makes the groups comparable, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the prompt. Before/after comparisons confound the change with seasonality, promotions, and traffic mix.

distractors.A: Calendar adjustments cannot remove other weekly differences such as campaigns or product launches, so the comparison remains confounded.
distractors.C: Impressions from reviewers are subjective and not tied to the conversion metric under test.
distractors.D: Choosing the busiest hours selects a non-representative slice and confounds time of day with the prompt.

scenario: A fintech compares two Claude prompts for classifying customer disputes. After 40 conversations per variant, variant B is correct 55% of the time versus 50% for variant A, and the product owner wants to declare B the winner.
stem: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Declare B the winner, since any improvement is worth shipping if the change cost nothing.
Declare A the winner, since it was the incumbent and the gap is below ten percentage points.
Switch to a larger judge model so that the 5-point gap becomes statistically significant.
Treat it as inconclusive; size the test from the baseline rate and smallest effect worth detecting.

rationale.correct: With 40 samples per arm, a 5-point gap is well within random variation. A proper test fixes the sample size in advance from the baseline rate, the minimum effect that matters, and the desired confidence.

distractors.A: A small gap on a small sample can easily be chance, and shipping on it risks acting on noise.
distractors.B: Defaulting to the incumbent because a gap looks small is also a judgment on noise, not a statistical conclusion.
distractors.C: Changing the judge does not create information; significance depends on sample size and variance, not on the grader choice.

scenario: A hospital group wants to replace the model behind its patient-message triage with a newer one. The offline eval looks good, but patient-facing errors are costly and the team cannot expose any patient to untested behavior.
stem: Which rollout approach best fits?

options.text: Release to the whole patient base during a weekend, since lower traffic reduces the number of people affected.
Switch five percent of patients to the new model, since a small share limits the harm if it errs.
Run the new model in shadow mode on live traffic, logging its outputs unseen, and compare with the current model.
Release internally to staff for a week, then switch everyone, since staff will report any problems.

rationale.correct: Shadow mode exercises the new model on real inputs while users only ever see the current model's output, so no patient is exposed. A canary would expose some patients, which the constraint rules out.

distractors.A: A lower-traffic window reduces the count of affected patients but still exposes all of them to untested behavior.
distractors.B: A canary does expose that five percent of patients to untested behavior, which the stated constraint forbids.
distractors.D: Staff usage rarely resembles patient traffic, so the signal is weak and the final switch is still untested on patients.

scenario: A SaaS team runs an A/B test of two support prompts. After day three, the dashboard shows variant B ahead with p = 0.04, and a manager proposes stopping the test immediately to ship B. The team had planned to run for two weeks.
stem: What is the best course of action?

options.text: Stop now and ship B, since p below 0.05 means the difference is statistically significant.
Continue to the planned sample size and duration, since stopping at the first favorable look inflates false positives.
Restart the test with a lower significance threshold, since early peeking shows the test was set up wrongly.
Extend the test indefinitely until p falls below 0.01 so that the result is beyond doubt.

rationale.correct: Checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant reading inflates the false-positive rate. The planned sample size and a full weekly cycle should be completed unless a sequential method designed for early stopping is used.

distractors.A: The nominal p-value assumes a single pre-planned look; repeated peeking makes it overstate the evidence.
distractors.C: Changing the threshold after seeing data is itself post-hoc and does not fix the peeking issue.
distractors.D: Running until a stricter value is reached is another data-dependent stopping rule and biases the result.

scenario: An education company A/B tests two tutoring assistants. Conversations span several sessions per student over weeks. The first design assigns each new session randomly to variant A or B.
stem: What is the main flaw, and the fix?

options.text: Sessions are the wrong unit because a student sees both variants; assign by student and keep that assignment sticky.
The variants will be unevenly distributed; assign sessions alternately to keep equal group sizes.
Random assignment is unnecessary for tutoring; use the students' teacher to choose a variant for each class.
Multi-session designs cannot be tested; evaluate a single first session for each student.

rationale.correct: If one student experiences both variants, effects carry over and the observations are not independent. Randomizing by the unit that experiences the treatment (the student) and keeping it fixed keeps the arms clean.

distractors.B: Strict alternation is predictable and still mixes variants within a student; balanced sizes do not fix contamination.
distractors.C: Teacher-chosen assignment introduces selection bias, since teachers may route stronger classes to a favored variant.
distractors.D: Looking only at the first session discards the long-term outcome the study is about, and avoiding the design does not solve it.

scenario: A bank cut costs by moving a multi-step loan-eligibility agent from a larger Claude model to a smaller, cheaper one. The prompt was unchanged. Simple applications still pass, but accuracy on applications needing several dependent calculations fell sharply.
stem: What is the most likely diagnosis, and the best first step?

options.text: The API is returning degraded output under load; open a support ticket and wait for the provider to fix it.
The prompt has decayed over time; rewrite it from scratch and redeploy it on the smaller model without further testing.
A model-capability mismatch on complex cases; evaluate both models by complexity and route hard cases to the larger one.
The agent's tools are now too numerous; remove half of them at random until accuracy recovers.

rationale.correct: Only the model changed, and failures concentrate in the hardest cases, which points to a capability mismatch. Running the same eval by complexity confirms it and supports a routing decision that keeps the cost saving for easy cases.

distractors.A: Failures correlate with task complexity, not with load or time, so a service degradation is unlikely to be the cause.
distractors.B: Prompts do not decay on their own; rewriting without evidence changes two things and cannot confirm the cause.
distractors.D: Nothing about the tool set changed; removing tools at random is guesswork that can break working behavior.

scenario: A healthcare FAQ assistant sometimes answers in two sentences and sometimes in three paragraphs for similar questions. The system prompt says 'Keep answers brief' near the top and, further down, 'Always explain your reasoning thoroughly so patients understand.'
stem: What is the most probable root cause, and the fix?

options.text: The model is non-deterministic by nature; set temperature to its minimum and accept the remaining variation.
The two instructions conflict, so length varies with how the model resolves them; reconcile into one length policy.
The model cannot follow length guidance; move to a larger model tier to get consistent output length.
The patients' questions are too varied; restrict the assistant to a fixed list of approved questions.

rationale.correct: Contradictory instructions give the model no consistent target, and variation in how it resolves the conflict shows up as inconsistent length. Reading the prompt for conflicts and stating one explicit policy is the right first fix.

distractors.A: Low temperature reduces variation but does not resolve a contradiction in the instructions themselves.
distractors.C: The behavior is explained by the prompt; changing models would not remove the conflict.
distractors.D: Restricting questions treats a prompt defect as an input problem and removes the assistant's value.

scenario: A telecom support bot sends a 7,000-token policy block in the system prompt on every request and marks it for caching. Usage logs show cache_read_input_tokens is zero on nearly every call. An engineer notices the first line of the system prompt is 'Current time: <timestamp>'.
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Increase max_tokens so that the cached portion has room to be stored with each response.
Shorten the policy block to under 1,000 tokens, since long prompts cannot be cached at all.
Move the current time out of the cached prefix, placing it after the last cache breakpoint.
Switch to a larger model, since cache hits depend on the model recognizing repeated text.

rationale.correct: Caching is a prefix match: a timestamp at the start changes the prefix on every request and invalidates the cache. Keeping stable content first and putting volatile values after the breakpoint restores cache reads.

distractors.A: max_tokens limits output length and has no effect on whether the input prefix is cached.
distractors.B: Long prefixes are what caching is for; the issue is a changing prefix, not its length.
distractors.D: Cache hits depend on the byte-identical prefix, not on model capability, and the cache is model-scoped anyway.

scenario: An airline's chatbot sends every request, including 'what is the baggage allowance?' and 'is my flight on time?', to its largest model. Analysis of a month of traffic shows about 70% of requests are short FAQs, and the remaining 30% need multi-step reasoning over bookings.
stem: Which approach best improves cost without harming quality?

options.text: Move the whole workload to the smallest model, since the majority of requests are simple.
Route FAQs to a smaller model, validate on the eval set, keep complex requests on the larger.
Randomly assign half of the requests to a smaller model to see whether anyone complains.
Cap the output length on each request to 50 tokens.

rationale.correct: Routing matches model capability to task difficulty, saving cost on the common simple case while protecting hard cases. Validating the router and the smaller model on the eval set confirms quality holds.

distractors.A: A uniform switch puts the 30% of complex requests on a model that may fail them, with no evidence.
distractors.C: Random assignment by difficulty-blind coin flip exposes complex cases to the weaker model and measures only complaints.
distractors.D: A blanket 50-token cap truncates the complex answers and degrades quality instead of reducing waste.

scenario: A retailer's product-description assistant returns 800-token responses with background paragraphs, but the page only displays about 100 tokens of copy. Output tokens drive most of the bill and the response time.
stem: What is the most appropriate change?

options.text: Ask for the exact short format in the prompt with structured output; keep max_tokens as a safety cap.
Set max_tokens to 100, so that the response is cut off at the displayed length.
Ask for longer answers and truncate them in the page template, to keep the model's reasoning intact.
Move to a larger model, since stronger models generate fewer tokens for the same request.

rationale.correct: Output is priced and takes time per token, so the lever is to ask for the needed format. A safety cap guards runaway output, but the length should be shaped by instructions, not by truncation.

distractors.B: A hard cut at 100 tokens ends responses mid-sentence (stop_reason max_tokens) instead of producing a complete short answer.
distractors.C: Generating text that is discarded pays for tokens and time that deliver no value.
distractors.D: A larger model does not inherently produce shorter output, and it costs more per token.

scenario: An internal legal-research tool is used sporadically. Each query sends the same 20,000-token reference corpus, and users typically return after 15 to 30 minutes. The team enabled prompt caching with the default settings, but the bill barely dropped and cache writes appear on most requests.
stem: What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Add a second cache breakpoint at the end of the user's question to cache more of each request.
Send a throwaway request each minute to keep the default cache alive around the clock.
Reduce the corpus to 2,000 tokens so each request costs less even without a cache hit.
Use the longer cache time-to-live, because the default entry expires between requests.

rationale.correct: The default cache lifetime is short and requests here arrive after longer gaps, so each request pays the write premium and never reads. A longer time-to-live fits the gap, and reads then cost far less than uncached input.

distractors.A: The user's question differs on each request, so caching it adds writes with no later reads.
distractors.B: Keep-alive pings every minute spend tokens around the clock for a tool used sporadically, likely costing more than it saves.
distractors.C: Cutting the corpus by 90% sacrifices the research content that the tool exists to provide.

scenario: A health system ships a revised prompt for its patient-message assistant on Tuesday. The pre-release eval passed, but the team has been burned before by regressions that only showed up in real traffic days later. Ops wants an early-warning mechanism for the first week after each release.
stem: Which operating practice best provides that early warning?

options.text: Wait for the monthly business review and compare total conversation counts before and after the release.
Compare sampled quality and thumbs-down rate with the prior version's baseline, alerting beyond a set margin.
Alert whenever the average response length of the new version differs from that of the old version.
Re-run the full pre-release eval suite once the first customer complaint has been escalated to the team.

rationale.correct: Scoring a sample of live traffic and tracking feedback by prompt version, with an agreed alert margin against the baseline, detects a real-traffic regression within days of release, using the same quality signals as the eval but on production inputs.

distractors.A: Conversation counts measure demand, not quality, and a monthly review is too slow to catch a first-week regression.
distractors.C: Length changes are a weak proxy: quality can fall without a length change, and benign rewording would page the team needlessly.
distractors.D: Waiting for an escalated complaint makes users the detector, and the pre-release suite already passed, so re-running it adds no new information.

scenario: A retailer's Claude service has an on-call rotation. The team wants alerts that catch real customer impact without paging for every transient error. Today the system pages on any non-200 response from the API.
stem: Which alerting approach is best?

options.text: Keep paging on each non-200 response, since early notice of any failure is better.
Alert on just the number of tokens used per day, since usage reflects overall system health.
Disable paging and review a weekly dashboard, since transient API errors resolve themselves.
Alert on failure rate, p95 latency, and hourly cost over a window, each with an owner and runbook.

rationale.correct: Alerts should reflect service-level indicators over a window, so transient errors the client retries do not page anyone while sustained impact does. An owner and runbook make each alert actionable.

distractors.A: Per-response paging produces noise, including errors that retries already absorbed, leading to alert fatigue.
distractors.B: Token totals say little about failures or latency, so an outage could pass unnoticed.
distractors.C: A weekly review would leave a real outage unnoticed for days.

scenario: A catalog-tagging service has run for eight months with stable error rates and latency. The business recently added products from a new region with different language and category conventions, and merchandisers are now noticing worse tags. Dashboards show no alert.
stem: What monitoring would have caught this earliest?

options.text: Tracking the input mix alongside sampled quality by segment, compared with a baseline.
Monitoring request count per hour, since a drop in volume would show that tagging quality had degraded.
Tracking only the average output length, since length changes whenever the model's behavior changes.
Checking error rates more often, since errors rise whenever quality degrades.

rationale.correct: Quality drift usually arrives with a shift in the inputs. Tracking the input distribution and sampled quality per segment against a baseline reveals a new segment performing worse even when errors and latency are flat.

distractors.B: Volume does not change when quality changes; it measures demand, not correctness.
distractors.C: Output length is a weak proxy and can stay stable while tags are wrong.
distractors.D: The service returned valid responses, so error rates stay flat while tags quietly become wrong.

scenario: A bank's claims assistant has a thumbs-down button. Product reviews show 'thumbs-down' totals, but engineers cannot tell what went wrong in each case or add them to the regression tests.
stem: What is the best improvement to feedback capture?

options.text: Replace the button with a monthly survey to the full customer base, since surveys give more representative sentiment.
Record each rating with the request or trace ID and optional reason, so the full interaction can be retrieved and reviewed.
Remove the button and rely on call-center complaints, since complaints are more serious than ratings.
Store just the aggregated daily count of thumbs-down, since individual ratings are noisy.

rationale.correct: Feedback is only actionable if it can be tied to the exact prompt version, context, and response. Linking each rating to a trace lets the team review failures and promote them into the eval set.

distractors.A: A monthly survey is slower and detached from specific interactions, so cases cannot be investigated.
distractors.C: Complaints arrive late and sparsely, and still need a trace to be actionable.
distractors.D: Aggregated counts hide which interactions failed, which is the information needed to fix them.

scenario: An insurer's Claude pipeline classifies scanned claim letters. Accuracy is 95% on typed letters but 70% on scans from one branch office. The prompt and model are identical for both, and the classification labels for the failing scans were verified by adjusters.
stem: What should the team check first?

options.text: Whether the OCR text extracted from the scans is garbled or missing, since the model sees only that text.
Whether the model was silently updated, since accuracy can drop for one branch's traffic at a time.
Whether the labels are too strict, since adjusters at one branch may apply the categories differently.
Whether the temperature is too high for scanned letters, since scans contain more varied text than typed ones.

rationale.correct: The failure is confined to one input source with an identical prompt and model, so inspect what the model actually received. Garbled OCR text is an input-completeness problem, and no prompt or model change will recover information that was never delivered.

distractors.B: A model update would affect typed and scanned letters alike, not a single branch's scans.
distractors.C: The labels were verified by adjusters, and the gap tracks the input source rather than the label definitions.
distractors.D: Temperature is the same for both input types and would not produce a source-specific accuracy gap.

scenario: A retail analytics service asks Claude to 'return the result as JSON'. Most responses parse, but about 3% arrive wrapped in an introductory sentence or in a markdown fence, and the parser throws. stop_reason is end_turn on all of them.
stem: What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Constrain the output with structured outputs or a strict tool schema so the response is always valid against the schema.
Add the line 'Return only JSON, no commentary' three more times to the prompt so that the instruction is not missed.
Wrap the parser in a retry loop that resends the same request until the response happens to parse.
Raise max_tokens so that the model has room to finish the JSON after its introductory sentence.

rationale.correct: Format drift on a small share of responses is an enforcement problem, not an instruction problem. Schema-constrained output (structured outputs, or a strict tool) guarantees structurally valid responses, which instructions and retries only make more likely.

distractors.B: Repeating the instruction improves odds slightly but remains probabilistic, so occasional wrapped responses will persist.
distractors.C: Retrying until success spends tokens and latency on a deterministic-enough defect and still has no guarantee of ending.
distractors.D: The responses ended normally (end_turn), so truncation is not the cause and a larger limit has no effect.

scenario: A European retailer's chat assistant keeps conversation summaries in a vector store to personalize later chats. A customer submits a GDPR erasure request.
stem: Which design choice most directly makes honoring this request feasible?

options.text: Tell the assistant in its system prompt to forget a customer's data once that customer has asked to be forgotten.
Retain the summaries for possible disputes and mark the requesting customer's records as hidden from future retrieval.
Blend customers' summaries together into one shared index so that no single record is identifiable as personal data.
Key stored summaries and embeddings by customer ID so one request can delete everything derived from that customer.

rationale.correct: Erasure is only practical if personal data lives in stores you control and can locate by data subject, including derived artifacts such as embeddings. A deletion path keyed by customer ID makes the right enforceable in code.

distractors.A: The model has no persistent memory to instruct; the personal data sits in your stores, which a prompt cannot delete.
distractors.B: Hiding records does not erase them; the data is still held and still subject to the request.
distractors.C: Blending does not anonymize text that may still contain identifying details, and it makes later deletion of one person's data harder.

scenario: A clinic wants Claude to suggest billing codes from visit notes. The notes include full demographics, insurance details, and the clinician's free text. The clinic is subject to HIPAA.
stem: Which approach best applies the minimum necessary principle?

options.text: Send only the note sections needed for coding, with direct identifiers removed or tokenized where the task does not require them.
Send the full chart for maximum context, and tell the model in the system prompt to ignore demographic and insurance details.
Encrypt the full chart in transit, which meets the principle without changing what is sent to the model.
Send the full notes but cap the response length so little patient data can appear in the output.

rationale.correct: Minimum necessary means limiting the PHI disclosed to what the task requires. Filtering and tokenizing before the prompt is built reduces exposure at the source.

distractors.B: Telling the model to ignore data does not limit what is disclosed; the unneeded PHI is still sent and processed.
distractors.C: Encryption protects data in transit but does not reduce the amount of PHI disclosed, which is what the principle addresses.
distractors.D: Capping output length limits what comes back, not what was sent, so the unnecessary disclosure still happens.

scenario: A health-tech startup wants to prototype a note-summarization feature on real patient records. It plans to use an LLM service for which no business associate agreement (BAA) has been signed.
stem: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Use real records for the prototype since it is internal and not yet customer-facing.
Use real records after adding a system prompt line telling the model to treat all records as strictly confidential.
Prototype with synthetic or de-identified data until a BAA covering the service and use is in place.
Use real records since encryption in transit removes the need for an agreement with the vendor.

rationale.correct: A vendor that handles PHI on a covered entity's behalf generally must be covered by a BAA for that service before PHI is shared. Internal prototypes are not exempt, so use data that is not PHI until the agreement exists.

distractors.A: Internal use does not remove the requirement; sharing PHI with a vendor without a BAA is still a disclosure problem.
distractors.B: A confidentiality instruction to the model is not a contractual or regulatory safeguard for the vendor relationship.
distractors.D: Encryption in transit is a technical safeguard; it does not substitute for the agreement that governs the vendor's handling of PHI.

scenario: A federal agency plans an assistant over agency data whose sensitivity categorization is moderate. The team has selected a vendor endpoint and is ready to start building.
stem: What should the architect confirm first?

options.text: That the vendor's region is within the United States and that agency data is encrypted at rest and in transit.
That the chosen deployment path holds a FedRAMP authorization at the level the agency's data requires.
That a prototype can be built on the vendor's public endpoint now, with authorization handled in the final security review.
That the vendor holds a general security certification such as an independent audit report covering the service.

rationale.correct: Federal data at a given impact level generally must be processed in an environment authorized at that level. Confirming this up front avoids building on a path the agency cannot use.

distractors.A: Location and encryption are useful controls but do not establish that the environment is authorized for this data's level.
distractors.C: Deferring the check risks building real functionality, and possibly handling real data, on a path that cannot be approved.
distractors.D: Other certifications and audit reports can help but do not substitute for FedRAMP authorization at the required level.

scenario: A telecom launches a support assistant with a human-sounding name and persona. Customers sometimes ask, "Am I talking to a real person?"
stem: What should the design do?

options.text: Instruct the persona to say it is a member of the support team when asked, to avoid confusing customers.
Disclose up front that this is an AI assistant, and answer truthfully if a customer asks whether it is human.
Disclose in the terms of service, which is where the company keeps its other product disclosures for customers.
Disclose when a customer is visibly upset or confused, since that is when the question matters most to them.

rationale.correct: Transparency means people know when they are dealing with an AI, and a sincere question deserves a truthful answer. A persona is fine for tone, but it should not be used to deceive.

distractors.A: Claiming to be human deceives customers and undermines trust; a persona should not extend to misrepresenting what the system is.
distractors.C: A terms-of-service line is easy to miss and does not make the interaction itself transparent.
distractors.D: Disclosing only to upset customers leaves everyone else uninformed and is an unreliable trigger.

scenario: An HR team plans a Claude assistant that summarizes candidate profiles for recruiters. Before launch, the architect must decide how to test for bias.
stem: Which test is most informative?

options.text: Run matched pairs of profiles differing only in demographic signals such as names, and compare outcomes across groups.
Check that the system prompt tells the model to treat all candidates equally, and review the wording.
Remove names and photos from résumés and treat the system as unbiased, since protected attributes are no longer present.
Measure agreement with recruiters' past decisions and launch if agreement exceeds 90% on a held-out set.

rationale.correct: A counterfactual matched-pair test isolates the effect of the demographic signal, so systematic differences in output point to bias that can be measured and addressed.

distractors.B: An instruction states intent but is not evidence about behavior; bias has to be measured on outputs.
distractors.C: Proxies such as school, location, or writing style can still carry demographic information, so removing names does not prove fairness.
distractors.D: Agreement with past decisions can reproduce the bias in those decisions, so high agreement is not evidence of fairness.

scenario: A hospital network deploys a Claude-based tool that drafts triage priority suggestions for nurses. Nurses ask what the tool is meant for, where it is known to be weaker, and how it performed for different patient groups.
stem: Which transparency artifact best serves the nurses?

options.text: A summary stating the tool's overall accuracy and the hospital's commitment to responsible AI use.
The full system prompt and source code, shared with the nursing staff for their inspection.
A use-and-limitations note with intended use, known failure modes, and results by patient group.
A description of how the underlying model was trained, supplied by the model provider.

rationale.correct: Transparency to users means telling them what the system is for, where it is weak, and how it performs for the groups they serve, so they can calibrate trust and spot problems. Documented evaluation results by group make that concrete.

distractors.A: Overall accuracy and values statements hide unequal performance and tell nurses nothing about where to be careful.
distractors.B: Prompt and code are not usable documentation for clinicians, and they show how the tool is built, not how well it works for each group.
distractors.D: Training information about a foundation model is general and does not describe this application's intended use or results.

scenario: A retailer built its support assistant's test set from last year's chat logs, which came almost entirely from existing English-speaking customers. It now plans to launch in two new markets with different languages and customer profiles.
stem: What is the best way to extend the evaluation before launch?

options.text: Add test cases that represent each new segment, with enough samples per segment to compare results between them.
Enlarge the existing test set tenfold with more English logs, so overall accuracy is measured more precisely.
Launch to the new markets and rely on the existing overall accuracy until users report problems.
Machine-translate the English test set into the new languages and treat the results as representative.

rationale.correct: A test set only describes the population it samples. Fairness across groups needs representative cases for each segment, including ones not yet served, in numbers large enough to compare.

distractors.B: A larger sample of the same population improves precision for that population but says nothing about the new segments.
distractors.C: Waiting for complaints shifts the discovery of unequal quality onto the users affected.
distractors.D: Translated English cases miss local phrasing, topics, and customer profiles, so they can hide real gaps.

scenario: After launch, an audit of a Claude-assisted tenant-screening tool shows noticeably lower approval rates for applicants from certain neighborhoods. Leadership asks for an immediate response.
stem: Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt telling the model not to be biased, and close the ticket as resolved.
Quantify the disparity from logged outcomes, add interim human review, and add cases to regression tests.
Take no action until an applicant files a formal complaint that the company can verify.
Retrain the underlying Claude model on a debiased dataset that the team curates in-house.

rationale.correct: Responding to bias means measuring it, limiting harm while a fix is developed, and building tests so it does not recur. Interim human review protects applicants during the remediation.

distractors.A: A generic instruction is unverified and does not measure or limit the harm already identified.
distractors.C: Waiting for a complaint ignores strong internal evidence and leaves applicants affected in the meantime.
distractors.D: Retraining a foundation model is not the proportionate first response for an application team; measurement, prompt and data changes, routing, and review come first.

scenario: An insurer uses Claude to help review claims. Some claims are denied, and customers have no way to contest the outcome.
stem: Which addition best supports fair outcomes?

options.text: An appeal path to a human reviewer who has the authority to override the AI-assisted decision.
Let the model re-evaluate a denied claim a second time whenever the customer objects.
Publish the system's overall accuracy figure on the website in place of an appeals process.
Allow appeals for claims above a dollar threshold, to control reviewer cost.

rationale.correct: Fair treatment of individuals affected by automated decisions includes meaningful redress. A human with real authority can correct errors the system cannot see in itself.

distractors.B: A second pass by the same system tends to repeat its first decision and is not independent review.
distractors.C: An aggregate statistic says nothing about the customer's own case and gives them no recourse.
distractors.D: Limiting appeals to large claims leaves customers with small claims, and any systematic errors in them, without redress.

scenario: A legal-research agent has a fetch tool that retrieves web pages. The team's system prompt tells the agent to fetch only from approved legal publishers, but logs show it occasionally fetches other domains found in the documents it reads.
stem: Which change most reliably enforces the restriction?

options.text: Expand the system prompt with the full list of approved publishers and repeat the restriction at the end of the prompt.
Enforce a domain allowlist inside the fetch tool and have it return a clear error for any other host.
Add a second Claude call that reviews each planned fetch and approves it if the domain looks reputable.
Review the fetch logs each week and remove access for any domain that was fetched without authorization.

rationale.correct: A restriction that must always hold belongs in code at the tool boundary, where it applies regardless of what the model decides or what injected content suggests.

distractors.A: A longer or repeated instruction reduces violations but is still probabilistic and can be overridden by content in documents.
distractors.C: A second model call adds cost and latency and can misjudge a domain; it is a judgment, not a deterministic control.
distractors.D: Weekly review is detective: unauthorized fetches have already happened before access is removed.

scenario: A tax-preparation assistant answers questions about current filing thresholds using only the model's built-in knowledge. Users report that some thresholds it states are out of date, though the answers sound confident.
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Tell the assistant in the system prompt to double-check each number before it answers.
Switch to a larger model tier, since a more capable model will know the current thresholds.
Retrieve current thresholds from an authoritative, dated source and have the assistant cite it.
Lower the sampling randomness so that the assistant gives the same threshold each time.

rationale.correct: Model knowledge has a cutoff and can be stale, and fluent confidence does not indicate currency. Grounding in a current authoritative source, with citation, makes answers verifiable.

distractors.A: The model cannot check numbers it has no current source for, so the instruction does not add information.
distractors.B: A larger model can still lack information after its knowledge cutoff, and capability does not make it current.
distractors.D: Lower randomness makes the same stale answer more repeatable but does not make it correct.

scenario: A code-review assistant correctly flags a race condition. The developer replies that the code is fine and was approved by a senior engineer, and the assistant withdraws the finding. Later the race condition causes an outage.
stem: Which risk does this illustrate, and what is the best mitigation?

options.text: Hallucination; require the assistant to cite the lines of code in every finding it reports.
Non-determinism; run each review three times and keep the findings that appear most often.
Context overflow; summarize the conversation after each reply so that the earlier finding is not lost.
Sycophancy; test with pushback cases and keep verification of findings independent of the author's reaction.

rationale.correct: Models can defer to a user's pushback even when they were right. Include challenge scenarios in evaluation and make acceptance of a finding depend on evidence or tests, not on the conversation's social pressure.

distractors.A: Citing lines helps grounding but does not stop the model from withdrawing a valid, cited finding under pressure.
distractors.B: Voting across runs does not help when each run is subject to the same deference once the developer pushes back.
distractors.C: The finding was not lost from context; the model reversed it, so summarizing would not change the behavior.

scenario: A research assistant produces reports with footnoted citations. A reviewer finds that several citations name plausible-looking papers that do not exist, though the report claims they support specific statements.
stem: What is the most reliable control?

options.text: Resolve each citation against a bibliographic database in code and drop or flag any that cannot be verified.
Add an instruction that every citation must be real and must be double-checked before it is written.
Ask a second Claude instance to confirm that each cited paper exists before the report is released.
Add a footer stating that the citations may be inaccurate and should be checked by the reader.

rationale.correct: Fabricated references are a known failure mode. A deterministic lookup against an authoritative source verifies existence independent of the model's fluency.

distractors.B: The model has no way to verify existence from memory, so the instruction changes little.
distractors.C: A second model has the same limitation and may confirm a plausible but invented title.
distractors.D: A disclaimer moves the checking burden to the reader and does not reduce the number of false citations.

scenario: A clinic's Claude-based note assistant is covered by the clinic's HIPAA compliance program. Engineers keep every prompt and response, which include PHI, in the debug log indefinitely.
stem: What is the best change?

options.text: Keep the logs but encrypt them, and give the engineering team access so that debugging is not slowed down.
Log minimal metadata, mask PHI in retained text, and set a retention period with restricted access.
Keep the logs but move them to a cheaper archive tier, since cost is the main risk.
Delete the existing logs immediately, and turn off logging for the assistant going forward.

rationale.correct: PHI in logs is still PHI. Minimum necessary, retention limits, and access control apply to logs too, while the team still needs enough information to debug and audit.

distractors.A: Encryption helps, but broad access to indefinite PHI logs conflicts with minimum necessary and access control.
distractors.C: Tiering saves cost without addressing the exposure or the lack of a retention limit.
distractors.D: Removing all logging eliminates debugging and audit capability, which compliance programs also require.

scenario: A health insurer's sponsor asks for a Claude assistant that summarizes clinician notes for claims reviewers. The kickoff covered goals and timeline but nobody asked where the notes live or who may use them. You are planning the next discovery session.
stem: Which discovery gap is most likely to make the project infeasible if it stays unanswered?

options.text: Where the notes are stored, in what formats, who owns them, and whether their use is permitted
Which reviewer workflow steps the summaries must fit into, and the target turnaround per claim
Which adoption and satisfaction metrics will be reported to the sponsor after launch
Which Claude model tier fits the sponsor's first-year budget for the pilot

rationale.correct: Data availability, quality, ownership, and permitted use determine whether the solution is feasible and which access path, retrieval design, and controls it needs. Learning that notes are scanned images or cannot leave a system of record after design has started forces a rebuild.

distractors.B: Workflow and turnaround matter, but they can be adjusted by design; they do not decide whether the data can be used at all.
distractors.C: Reporting metrics can be settled any time before launch and do not affect feasibility.
distractors.D: Tier choice follows from requirements and measured evaluation, and it is easy to change later.

scenario: A state benefits agency wants a Claude chatbot to answer citizen questions. The sponsor's only quality requirement is "it must be accurate." The design team is about to start building.
stem: What is the best next step in discovery?

options.text: Select the most capable model available so that accuracy is not a concern
Agree with owners what counts as a correct answer, then grade a test set of real citizen questions
Agree a target of 99 percent accuracy on a sample of questions and begin building
Benchmark candidate models on a public question-answering leaderboard and use the top scorer

rationale.correct: "Accurate" cannot be checked until correctness is defined for this domain (policy-correct, current, cited) and measured on representative questions. That test set becomes the acceptance criterion for design and later for monitoring.

distractors.A: A larger model may help, but without a definition and a test set nobody can show the requirement was met.
distractors.C: A numeric target is a good start, but without a definition of a correct answer for this agency's policies the number cannot be measured consistently.
distractors.D: Public leaderboards measure generic tasks, not correctness on this agency's benefit rules.

scenario: A retailer's product owner supplied a requirements list for an assistant that drafts replies for 300 support agents. The list came entirely from managers; no agent, QA lead, or downstream CRM owner has been consulted.
stem: Which action would most improve the quality of the requirements?

options.text: Have Claude draft a fuller requirements list from the product owner's document for the managers to approve
Survey all 300 agents, asking them to rank the features on the managers' list
Observe agents at work and interview QA and the CRM owner to find workflow, edge cases, and integration limits
Ship a prototype to a small team and gather requirements from the complaints it produces

rationale.correct: Requirements come from the people who do the work and consume the output. Observing agents and speaking with QA and the CRM owner surfaces workflow details, quality bars, and integration limits that managers' summaries omit.

distractors.A: Claude can only restate what the document contains; it adds no knowledge from people who do the work.
distractors.B: Ranking the managers' list cannot reveal needs and constraints that are missing from it.
distractors.D: A prototype is useful later, but complaints as the elicitation method surfaces gaps late and at higher cost.

scenario: A bank wants Claude to extract fields from loan documents. The sponsor says the documents are "standard PDFs" and provides three clean examples. Operations staff mention that many arrive as phone photos and faxes.
stem: What should the architect do before committing to a design?

options.text: Choose an OCR vendor now, since image quality is the largest risk in the project
Build synthetic documents modeled on the clean examples to test extraction at scale
Design for clean PDFs now and add photos and faxes in a second release
Sample recent documents, including the worst-quality ones, and test extraction on them

rationale.correct: Feasibility depends on the real input distribution. A representative sample, including low-quality inputs, exposes format and quality issues early and gives measured numbers for accuracy, cost, and routing of difficult documents.

distractors.A: Picking a vendor before measuring real inputs may solve a problem that is smaller or larger than assumed.
distractors.B: Synthetic documents copy the sponsor's assumption instead of testing it.
distractors.C: Deferring other formats leaves a large share of real volume unaddressed and may invalidate the architecture.

scenario: An HR team tells you its policy assistant can make occasional mistakes because "employees double-check anything important." In a follow-up interview, HR business partners say managers have started quoting the assistant's answers in disciplinary meetings.
stem: How should discovery respond to this contradiction?

options.text: Record how answers are used, rate the cost of wrong answers by question type, and set thresholds to match
Keep the sponsor's stated tolerance for errors as the requirement, since the sponsor owns the business risk
Add a standing disclaimer that the assistant may be wrong to each answer it gives
Defer the question to the pilot, when real error rates will show how serious it is

rationale.correct: The cost of a wrong answer is a requirement that shapes accuracy targets, citation, human review, and scope. Discovery should capture real usage and stake levels, then derive controls per question type rather than rely on a blanket assumption.

distractors.B: The tolerance rested on an assumption that interviews showed to be false, so it cannot stand unchanged.
distractors.C: A disclaimer informs users but does nothing about high-stakes uses and shifts the risk onto employees.
distractors.D: Waiting lets the high-stakes use grow unobserved and delays controls that shape the design.

scenario: A CFO asks why the ticket-classification service runs on a mid-tier model rather than the most capable one. You have an evaluation set and a cost estimate for both options.
stem: How should you present the decision to the CFO?

options.text: Walk through how tokens are priced and why classification is a simple task for language models
Show cost per thousand tickets and measured accuracy for each option, and state the accuracy gain that would justify the higher spend
Explain that the most capable model is wasteful for a classification task, and that it should not be considered for this service at all
Offer to run the most capable model everywhere to remove the question of quality

rationale.correct: An executive decides on business outcomes. Cost per unit, measured quality for each option, and the break-even point for upgrading frame the trade-off in terms the CFO can act on.

distractors.A: Token pricing mechanics are detail the CFO did not ask about, and they do not show whether quality is acceptable.
distractors.C: Dismissing the alternative without evidence asks for trust rather than showing the trade-off, and the gap may matter for some ticket types.
distractors.D: Running the largest model everywhere avoids the discussion by accepting a cost that has not been justified by the measured gap.

scenario: Before approving a customer-support pilot, the security team asks the architect for a data-flow diagram of the Claude integration.
stem: What should the diagram and accompanying notes contain?

options.text: The vendor's published security whitepaper and a link to its documentation
The full system prompt text, together with the list of guardrail instructions and behavioral rules that are given to the model
The data sent to the model, trust boundaries, where data is stored or logged and for how long, and the controls at each hop
A product demo showing the assistant answering representative questions

rationale.correct: Security reviewers assess where sensitive data goes and what protects it. A data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, storage, retention, and controls answers that directly and makes gaps visible for review.

distractors.A: A vendor document describes the vendor's platform, not how this particular system moves and stores the company's data.
distractors.B: The prompt shows intent, but it says nothing about data movement, storage, or enforcement, and instructions are not security controls.
distractors.D: A demo shows functionality; it does not show data handling or the points at which controls apply.

scenario: Legal counsel asks whether the contract-summarization tool's output can be relied on without lawyer review. The pilot shows high average accuracy but a few clear errors on unusual clauses.
stem: What is the most appropriate way to answer?

options.text: Describe limitations by clause type, plus the review, citations, and logging that limit the impact of errors
Say accuracy is high enough that review can be dropped once the pilot ends
Say reliability depends on final pilot accuracy, so legal should weigh in after the numbers are final
Point counsel to the system prompt, which tells the model to flag uncertain clauses

rationale.correct: Legal needs an honest account of where the system can fail and which controls limit the consequences. Stating limitations by clause type with review, citations, and an audit trail enables a real risk decision.

distractors.B: A high average hides the unusual clauses where errors cluster, and it removes the control that mitigates them.
distractors.C: Waiting excludes the party that owns this risk decision from shaping the controls while they can still be designed.
distractors.D: A prompt instruction to flag uncertain clauses is not a guaranteed control, so it does not describe how the risk is actually bounded.

scenario: Your team chose retrieval-augmented generation over fine-tuning for a policy assistant because policy documents change weekly and answers must cite current text. A new engineer will own the system and needs the reasoning recorded.
stem: Which architecture decision record entry is most useful?

options.text: Retrieval chosen: policies change weekly and answers need current citations; accepted costs are index upkeep and latency; revisit if that changes.
Fine-tuning was rejected because it costs far too much compared with retrieval for this project, and the budget owners did not want to fund it.
Retrieval was chosen because it is the common approach for knowledge assistants today.
Retrieval was chosen after a long discussion; see the project chat thread for the reasoning.

rationale.correct: A good record states the context, the decision, the alternatives and why they lost, and the consequences accepted, along with conditions for revisiting. This gives a successor the reasoning and the trigger for change.

distractors.B: An unquantified cost claim does not state the real driver, the data change rate, and omits the consequences accepted.
distractors.C: Popularity is not a reason tied to this system's constraints and gives a successor nothing to evaluate or revisit.
distractors.D: Pointing to a chat thread makes the reasoning hard to find and verify, and it disappears when the thread does.

scenario: A steering committee has ten minutes to decide between a single-agent and a multi-agent design. Your analysis is thorough and runs to forty pages.
stem: How should you structure the presentation?

options.text: Walk the committee through each of the architecture diagrams in detail, then arrive at a recommendation at the end of the session
Lead with a recommendation and the decision needed, compare the options on cost, risk, and time, and keep details in an appendix
Present only the recommended option so the discussion stays focused
Ask the committee which design they prefer and document the choice

rationale.correct: Executives need the decision and the basis for it. Leading with the recommendation, showing real alternatives with their trade-offs, and offloading detail to an appendix respects the time while keeping the reasoning inspectable.

distractors.A: Leading with diagrams spends the time on mechanics and risks the decision being deferred before the recommendation is reached.
distractors.C: Showing only one option hides the trade-offs and makes the recommendation harder to trust or challenge.
distractors.D: Asking for a preference hands a technical choice to people without the analysis and avoids giving an architect's recommendation.

scenario: To reduce cost, the architect designed a reporting workflow to run as asynchronous batch processing, so results will arrive within hours rather than seconds. Build has not started, and the business unit that uses the reports was not part of the discussion.
stem: What should the architect do now?

options.text: Record the trade-off in the architecture notes and announce it in the release communication before launch
Revert to real-time processing until the business unit has been consulted
Explain what changes for the unit, such as when results arrive, and get its acceptance before building
Offer the unit a larger model for the batch run, to compensate for the slower turnaround it will see

rationale.correct: A trade-off that changes what users experience must be communicated in the users' terms, and accepted by the owners of the affected workflow, before it is built. Cost savings are real only if the business can work with the delay.

distractors.A: Documentation and a release announcement tell the unit after the choice is final, taking away its chance to object or adapt.
distractors.B: Reverting discards a legitimate saving and prevents a joint decision on whether the delay is tolerable.
distractors.D: A larger model does not shorten turnaround and adds cost, which undermines the reason for the change.

scenario: A COO wants the contract-summarization service to carry a "100 percent accuracy" SLA before rollout. The system is built on Claude and graded on a golden set of 300 contracts.
stem: How should the architect respond?

options.text: Sign the SLA and add financial penalties so the team is motivated to reach it
Decline to commit to any quality number at all, on the basis that generative output cannot be measured in a reliable or repeatable way
Set the sampling temperature to its lowest value and then commit to the SLA
Propose measurable targets, such as accuracy on critical fields graded on sampled production output, with human review for the rest

rationale.correct: Probabilistic systems can be held to measurable service objectives, not guarantees of perfection. Defining targets by field importance, measuring them on sampled production output, and pairing them with review and escalation gives the COO something enforceable.

distractors.A: A penalty does not make perfection achievable; it moves risk to the team without changing what the system can do.
distractors.B: Quality can be measured with a graded sample, so refusing any number discards a workable tool and offers the COO nothing.
distractors.C: Lower sampling temperature reduces variation but does not make the output correct, so it cannot support a perfection guarantee.

scenario: A customer contract for a Claude-powered chat assistant requires "responses within 2 seconds." Replies range from one sentence to several paragraphs, and the assistant streams its output.
stem: How should the latency commitment be defined?

options.text: As the average total response time across the requests in a month
As the 95th-percentile time to the first streamed token, tracked separately from total completion time
As the maximum total response time for any single request in a given month
As the median total response time, calculated for short replies, because those are the easiest to control

rationale.correct: For streamed interactive output, perceived responsiveness is the time to first token, and a percentile target sets expectations for the tail. Total time depends on reply length and should be tracked separately, not promised as a single figure.

distractors.A: An average hides slow requests and mixes short and long replies, so it does not match what users experience.
distractors.C: A maximum for any single request is not achievable for variable-length generation and would be breached by long replies.
distractors.D: Measuring only short replies selects the easy cases and misrepresents the service for most users.

scenario: Users rate a claims-assistant's answers with thumbs up or down. The support lead wants each thumbs-down fixed the same day by editing the production prompt.
stem: What is the best way to handle this feedback?

options.text: Edit the production prompt whenever a complaint arrives, so that the affected user sees a quick improvement on the same day
Ignore the thumbs-down ratings because user opinion is too subjective to act on
Triage feedback into a backlog, add representative cases to the evaluation set, and ship changes through the regular gated release
Act only on feedback from senior stakeholders, whose judgment is more reliable

rationale.correct: Feedback is a source of test cases. Triaging it, adding representative cases to the evaluation set, and releasing changes through a gate lets improvements be verified against regressions rather than fixing one complaint at the expense of others.

distractors.A: Editing the live prompt per complaint skips evaluation, risks regressions elsewhere, and leaves no versioned record to roll back.
distractors.B: Ratings are noisy individually but informative in aggregate, and dismissing them removes the main signal of real-world quality.
distractors.D: Filtering by seniority biases the signal toward a few users and misses the failures experienced by the people actually using the system.

scenario: A bank asks for 99.99 percent availability on an assistant that depends on the Claude API and a retrieval service. The team's own services are well within that range.
stem: What is the most defensible commitment?

options.text: Set an availability objective for what the team controls, design retries and a fallback path, and state the dependencies' impact on the error budget
Commit to the provider's published figure for the model API alone
Commit to 99.99 percent, since the team's own services meet it
Avoid stating any availability figure, because the third-party dependencies are outside the team's control and could make any number untrue

rationale.correct: A commitment cannot exceed what the dependency chain supports. Setting an objective for the controllable part, adding retries, queueing, or a degraded mode, and showing how upstream outages consume the budget makes the promise realistic and the risk visible.

distractors.B: The provider's figure covers only one component and ignores the retrieval service and the application, so it does not describe the assistant.
distractors.C: The team's own uptime ignores upstream dependencies, so the end-to-end figure would be lower than promised.
distractors.D: Declining to give any figure fails the stakeholder's need for a commitment and ignores that fallbacks can improve user-visible availability.

scenario: During a pilot, employees keep asking the HR assistant about payroll tax advice, which is outside its scope, and then rate the assistant poorly when it declines.
stem: What is the best action?

options.text: Widen the assistant's scope so it attempts the tax and legal questions employees keep asking
State scope and limits at onboarding and in the UI, redirect out-of-scope questions, and track their volume
Exclude out-of-scope ratings from the pilot report and report quality on in-scope questions alone
Add a standard apology message to each decline and revisit the ratings once the assistant has launched

rationale.correct: Unmet expectations are managed by stating what the system does and does not do, handling out-of-scope questions gracefully, and measuring how often they occur. The count also informs whether scope should later change on evidence.

distractors.A: Expanding scope to topics without sources or review adds risk and does not close the expectation gap.
distractors.C: In-scope reporting is useful, but dropping the ratings hides the expectation gap and the demand signal about scope.
distractors.D: An apology message does not tell users what the assistant covers or where to go, and waiting leaves the perception to harden.

scenario: A product director notices that asking the assistant the same question twice yields different wording and calls this a defect. The two answers contain the same facts and recommended action.
stem: How should the architect respond?

options.text: Promise that setting temperature to zero will guarantee identical text on each call to the API
Explain that wording varies, and measure consistency where it matters, such as the same decision or facts, with an agreed tolerance
Cache the first response for each question permanently, so that users see exactly the same text whenever they repeat a question
Tell the director that variation is a model limitation and nothing can be done

rationale.correct: Generative systems may vary wording even when decisions are stable. The expectation to set is consistency in the outcome, such as the classification or cited facts, checked on repeated runs, with a tolerance both sides accept.

distractors.A: Low temperature reduces variation but does not guarantee identical output, so the promise could not be kept.
distractors.C: Permanent caching freezes stale or wrong answers and does not address consistency for new or reworded questions.
distractors.D: Variation can be managed through prompt design, structured outputs, and measurement, so saying nothing can be done is inaccurate.

scenario: A consultancy is handing a Claude-based document pipeline to a client's on-call operations team, who have never operated an LLM system. You are drafting the runbook.
stem: Which runbook entry would be the most useful at 3 a.m.?

options.text: An overview of how large language models generate text and why they sometimes err
A link list to the vendor's API documentation and the model's release notes
A description of the pipeline's design goals and the reasoning behind each architectural choice, written by the original architects
A symptom-triggered entry, such as a spike in 429 errors, with diagnostic steps, the owner, and rollback steps for the prompt or model version

rationale.correct: Runbooks are used under pressure. Entries keyed to observable symptoms, with diagnosis, ownership, and a rollback procedure for the versioned prompt and model configuration, let an operator act without prior LLM expertise.

distractors.A: A conceptual overview is useful training, but it does not tell an operator what to check or do during an incident.
distractors.B: External links push the operator to search documentation while the incident runs and do not describe this system's specific response.
distractors.C: Design rationale belongs in the architecture documentation; during an incident the operator needs actions, not history.

scenario: A Claude pipeline for processing support tickets is moving to an operations team. The business case set a cost ceiling per processed ticket, but the handoff documents contain no cost assumptions.
stem: What should be added to the handoff documentation?

options.text: Last month's invoice for the pilot and a link to the billing dashboard showing spend by project
Per-feature token budgets, the assumed cost per transaction, and how spend is monitored against them
A ranked list of cheaper models to switch to if spend rises above the forecast, with their prices
A summary of current pricing for each Claude model as of the handoff date, with sources

rationale.correct: Operators can detect cost drift only if they know what to expect. Documenting token budgets, cost-per-transaction assumptions, and the monitoring approach makes deviation visible and gives the team a basis for investigation.

distractors.A: A past invoice shows what was spent, but not what spend was expected, so operators cannot judge drift.
